title.$t: Roman Britannia, Part IV: The Long Goodbye

content.$t:
How Rome left Britain, and what it left behind- The End of Roman Britannia and the work of the giants.

In 410 CE, an emperor hiding in Ravenna sent a letter to Britain's cities with a simple message: look to your own defense. But Rome's exit isn't a sudden collapse; it is a tale of ambitious usurpers slowly bleeding the island of its legions to fight for the throne.

From the elevation of an ordinary soldier to the arrival of Anglo-Saxons who wandered through the ruins, Part IV explores the melancholic end of an empire and the "work of giants" it left behind.

Coin of Constantine III, 407–411 CE. An ordinary soldier elevated by the British legions because of his name.

In short

  • From Carausius in 287 CE to Magnus Maximus in 383 CE, Britain’s armies kept crossing the Channel to make emperors.
  • After 306 CE, Constantine the Great took British legions east. They were never fully replaced, but Christianity stayed.
  • In 407 CE, the legions chose a soldier named Constantine. Constantine III took the last garrison to Gaul and was executed in 411.
  • Around 410 CE, Emperor Honorius told Britain’s cities to defend themselves. Roman Britain ended with a letter, not a battle.
  • Anglo-Saxon settlers found the ruins and, in the Old English poem The Ruin, called them enta geweorc, “the work of giants”.

407 CE: A Military Camp in Northern Britannia

It had happened before. That was the point.

The legions of Britain had done this twice already in the past year alone. They had raised a soldier named Marcus on a shield and called him emperor. When Marcus disappointed them, they killed him and raised a man named Gratian.

When Gratian disappointed them within four months, they killed him too. Now they needed a third candidate.

The Western Empire was collapsing around them. Barbarians had crossed the frozen Rhine on the last day of 406 CE in the largest single migration the empire had ever seen. Gaul was burning. The legitimate emperor, Honorius, had retreated behind the impregnable marshes of Ravenna and showed no sign of coming out.

The British legions looked at the chaos across the Channel and made a decision. They wanted a name. Not a strategy. Not a general of proven brilliance. A name.

A century earlier, in this very province, a man named Constantine had been raised on a shield by British legions, and that Constantine had gone on to conquer the entire Roman world. The soldiers of Britain had developed something close to a superstition about it.

The name felt like a formula. Raise a Constantine, win the world.

They looked around the camp. They found a soldier. An ordinary soldier, nobody famous, nobody distinguished, no military record that survives in any source. But his name was Constantine.

They raised him on a shield.

He immediately stripped the last garrison from the island, crossed the Channel, and was dead within four years.

Britain never got its soldiers back, and Roman Britannia died with Constantine the Third.

The formula had worked once. That was the problem. Once is enough to make a tradition, and traditions in the Roman army had a way of outlasting their reasons.

I. The Pattern: A Century of Warlords

Coin of Carausius, self-proclaimed Emperor of the Britannic Empire, 287–293 CE. A naval commander who held Britain and northern Gaul against Rome for nearly a decade.

The century between Albinus and Constantine III had confirmed, again and again, that Britain was less a province than a launching pad.

After the catastrophe of 197 CE, after Albinus’s army had been butchered at Lugdunum and the northern Wall stripped bare, it took the personal intervention of the emperor Septimius Severus to stabilize the province. He arrived in 208 CE, old and gouty, and launched brutal punitive campaigns deep into Scotland.

Septimius died in York in 211 CE, the same city where Constantine would later be proclaimed. His sons Caracalla and Geta promptly abandoned their father’s Scottish ambitions and made peace with the northern tribes.

However, the damage had been done. The northern tribes had seen the Wall empty. They burned the forts and proved the frontier was permeable. Rome had lost the psychological advantage it had spent decades building.

In 260 CE, a breakaway Gallic Empire briefly incorporated Britain into its territories, three separate emperors governing a rump western empire for fifteen years, while the legitimate court struggled in the east.

In 287 CE came the most audacious episode of all: a naval commander named Carausius, facing prosecution for corruption, declared himself emperor of Britain and northern Gaul. He issued his own coins. He maintained his own court. He controlled the Channel fleet and defied Rome for seven years until his own minister had him murdered.

His successor lasted another three years before the emperor Constantius, father of Constantine the Great, mounted a military expedition and brought Britain back under central control.

Each episode followed the same grammar. A strong commander. A large army. A fractured empire. A crossing of the Channel. And Britain, once again, was left to manage itself in the interim, stripped of soldiers, exposed to the north, working out its own arrangements.

The island was becoming adept at self-sufficiency. That would matter in the end.

II. The Emperor from the Island: Constantine and the Christian World

Chi-Rho mosaic, Hinton St Mary, Dorset, c.350 CE, British Museum. The earliest known image of Christ from Roman Britain.

Constantine the Great, proclaimed in York in 306 CE, changed the world. But what did he do for Britain?

The British Problem demanded it. Constantine could not stay in Britain and be content. The very pattern that had made him emperor made staying impossible. The Tetrarchy, the system of four co-emperors Diocletian designed to prevent exactly this kind of provincial coup, had given legitimate succession to Galerius, the senior Augustus in the east.

Statue of Constantine: a bronze statue of Constantine the Great in York, the very city where he was proclaimed emperor in 306 CE before marching south to claim the Roman world.

Galerius had not appointed Constantine. The British legions had. That made Constantine a usurper under Roman law, regardless of his father’s bloodline. His only path to legitimacy was conquest.

He had to take the whole empire or lose his head. The same isolation that made Britain a breeding ground for emperor-makers also made it a trap: a man proclaimed in York could be dismissed as a provincial warlord unless he moved fast, moved south, and proved himself in the arena that actually counted.

The British Problem, in other words, did not just create Constantine. It chased him out of Britain. The province that handed him his purple had to strip its legions to fund the campaign that would make him real. Britain lost its emperor the same way it always did, by having him cross the Channel and never come back.

In the short term, he left. Britain was the platform, not the destination. He took his British legions east, fought his way across Gaul and Italy, and in 312 CE at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome, defeated his last serious rival under the sign of the Chi-Rho, the Christian symbol he claimed had appeared to him in a vision the night before battle. He legalized Christianity, convened the Council of Nicaea, founded Constantinople, and became the most consequential emperor since Augustus.

Britain received Christianity in return. The faith had been spreading quietly through the province for decades. Roman Britain shifted from a province with a patchwork of mystery cults, local gods, and a growing Christian minority to a province with an established church.

Christianity would prove to be the most durable thing Rome left in Britain. Constantine’s conversion made it official.

Christian communities existed in the larger towns, and British bishops attended the Council of Arles in 314 CE. Long after the administrators left, the coins stopped coming, and the villas were stripped for building stone, the church remained.

But the legions Constantine took east in 306 CE were never fully replaced. The garrison thinned. The Wall was still manned, the towns still functioning, the villas still occupied, but the depth of military resources that made Britain feel like a functioning part of the empire was quietly, steadily ebbing.

III. Magnus Maximus: The Second March

Coin portrait of Magnus Maximus, proclaimed emperor by the British legions in 383 CE. Remembered in Wales as Macsen Wledig, the last Roman who felt like theirs.

The clearest preview of the end came in 383 CE.

Gratian was the son of Valentinian I, a competent soldier-emperor who had kept the western frontiers intact through sheer professional force of will. When Valentinian died in 375 CE, power in the west passed to Gratian, who was sixteen. He grew into a ruler not without ability, but he inherited an empire in crisis and possessed none of his father’s iron authority.

The catastrophe arrived in 378 CE. The Goths, granted refuge inside the Danube frontier by a corrupt Roman administration, rose in revolt. At the Battle of Adrianople, the eastern emperor Valens, Gratian’s uncle, rode into a Gothic ambush and was killed. The Roman army of the east was effectively destroyed. It was the Roman Empire's worst military defeat at the time.

What followed hardened the western legions' contempt for Gratian. He responded to the Gothic crisis not by crushing the Goths but by negotiating with them, granting them unprecedented terms in 382 CE that allowed them to settle as a semi-autonomous people and owe Rome only loose military service.

To soldiers who had spent their careers dying to hold the line, this looked like surrender. Worse still, in the eyes of the traditional army, was what Gratian surrounded himself with. He showed marked personal favor to a unit of Alanic cavalry, steppe nomads; dressing in their style, hunting with them, lavishing them with gifts. To the Roman soldiery, this was not merely eccentric. It was a humiliation. Their emperor preferred barbarians to them.

In Britain, Magnus Maximus watched all of this from the far end of the empire. He was a capable, experienced Spaniard, deeply popular with the troops who had served under him for years along the Wall. When the chance came, his soldiers made the familiar calculation and proclaimed him Augustus.

End of Roman Britannia, 383–410 CE.

Maximus crossed to Gaul, defeated and killed Gratian, and established himself as western emperor. He ruled competently for five years, governing from Trier, negotiating with the Franks and Visigoths, and holding the Rhine frontier against relentless pressure.

By most measures, Maximus was a better emperor than the man he replaced. But Maximus stripped Britain’s garrison to fight his continental war, and that came with a heavy price.

And in 388 CE, the eastern emperor Theodosius marched west, defeated him in battle, and had him executed. The troops Maximus had taken from Britain never returned.

The Western Empire he left behind was unstable and diminished. Gratian’s younger brother Valentinian II was restored as western emperor in name, but Theodosius held the real power. When Valentinian II was found dead in 392 CE, almost certainly murdered by his powerful Frankish general Arbogast, the general installed a pagan professor named Eugenius as a puppet emperor and governed through him.

Theodosius marched west again. At the Battle of the Frigidus in 394 CE, he defeated Arbogast and Eugenius in one of the century's most bitterly fought engagements. Eugenius was executed. Arbogast fell on his sword. Theodosius became, briefly, the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire alone.

He died in 395 CE, leaving the empire to his two young sons. Arcadius, seventeen, received the east. Honorius, ten years old, received the west. The division was supposed to be administrative, not permanent. It proved to be both. The empire was never reunified.

And the soldiers that Maximus had taken from Britain were gone, absorbed into continental wars, deployed along the Rhine and the Danube, buried on Italian hillsides. Britain would make do with what was left.

There was always somewhere the soldiers were needed more. The eastern frontier. The Danube. The Rhine. Gaul. Spain. Italy. Britain waited at the end of the list, and the list never got shorter.

IV. The Last Constantine: 407 CE

The Western Roman Empire, c.410 CE. Britain sits at the fraying edge of a world dissolving from within. Honorius told its cities to defend themselves. No reinforcements were promised. No governor was named. That was the last official communication.

Which brings us back to the ordinary soldier with the fortunate name.

By 407 CE, the Britain that remained was diminished. The great villa estates of the south were fewer and quieter than they had been a century before. Coin circulation had been steadily declining since the 360s.

The towns still stood. The Wall was still, nominally, garrisoned. The administrative structures of the Diocese of Britannia still functioned. But the connection to Rome was fraying at every edge, and everyone in the province who paid attention knew it.

Constantine III crossed to Gaul in 407 CE with what remained of Britain’s garrison. He had early success; he stabilized the Rhine frontier, smashed the previous winter, gathered support in Gaul and Spain, and for a moment looked like he might be the real thing. He controlled more territory than most of his predecessors.

Coins of Constantine III.

But 407 CE was also the year the Visigoths under Alaric were circling Italy. And in 410 CE came the event that stunned the Roman world: Alaric sacked Rome itself. The eternal city, symbol of everything the empire meant, fell to a barbarian army for the first time in eight hundred years. The psychological shock was total.

Jerome wrote from Bethlehem that he could not speak for tears. Augustine began writing The City of God, an entire theology designed to explain why Rome's fall did not mean the fall of meaning.

By 411 CE, Honorius's forces had captured and executed Constantine III. The soldiers he had taken from Britain were dead, dispersed, or absorbed into other units.

The Diocese of Britannia, four provinces, administered from London, garrisoned along Hadrian’s Wall, integrated into the tax system and economy of the western empire for nearly four centuries, quietly ceased to function as a Roman entity.

In that same catastrophic year of 410 CE, the emperor Honorius sent a letter to the cities of Britain. The letter told the British cities to defend themselves.

No reinforcements were promised. No new governor was appointed. No timeline was given for restoring Roman authority. In the precise, bureaucratic language of imperial administration, the letter told the cities of Britain they were on their own.

That was all. This is how Roman Britannia ended. Not with a battle. Not with an invasion.

With a letter. With silence. With the slow absence of the coins that no longer arrived on the supply ships that no longer came.

V. The Silence and What Followed

Portchester Castle, Hampshire, a Saxon Shore fort built by the Romans c.285 CE to defend against Germanic raiders.

The fall of Roman Britain was not an event. It was a slow, uneven process, stretching across generations and visible only in retrospect.

The towns did not immediately empty. The villas did not immediately collapse. The roads kept working because roads keep working; they require no maintenance to remain usable for decades.

The Christian church survived better than the imperial administration that had legitimized it. The language shifted gradually, British Latin giving way to the older Celtic tongues, then, over the following centuries, to the Germanic dialects of newcomers from across the North Sea.

The newcomers had been coming for years. Germanic warriors- Angles, Saxons, Jutes, Frisians- had been raiding the eastern coast of Britain for generations.

The Romans had called this coastline the Saxon Shore and built a chain of massive forts specifically to defend against them. Now no one manned the forts. The walls still stood. The gates still swung. But the garrison was gone, and the coast was open.

Some came as raiders. Some came as settlers, invited by sub-Roman British rulers who needed warriors and had land to offer. Some came simply because the land was available and no organized military force was defending it. The process took generations, not years. In the west, Wales, Cornwall, Cumbria, parts of the north, Romano-British culture persisted for a century or more after the administrative end of Roman rule.

But across the lowland east, the heartland of Roman Britain, the land of villas and forums and heated floors and colonnaded basilicas, the transformation was eventually total.

The towns were gradually abandoned or occupied in ways that left no trace in the Roman building stock. The villas fell into disrepair, their roofs collapsing inward, their mosaic floors buried under the slow accumulation of rubble, soil, and time. The forum of Londinium, once the largest north of the Alps, became a field.

And then the Anglo-Saxons walked among the ruins.

VI. The Work of Giants

The Great Bath, Aquae Sulis (Bath), Somerset. The sacred hot springs channeled, roofed, and monumentalized by Rome. The steam never stopped rising. The people who built the roof were gone before anyone thought to write their names down.

They didn't know who built them.

The Anglo-Saxon settlers who moved through the abandoned landscapes of what had been Roman Britain looked at the stone walls, the crumbling basilicas, the bathhouses with their mysterious underfloor cavities, and the great roads running straight and true to the horizon, with no framework for understanding any of it.

Nothing in their world was built from dressed stone. Nothing in their experience suggested that human hands could have raised structures on this scale.

They called them enta geweorc. The work of giants.

An anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet, writing sometime in the 8th or 9th century, three hundred years after the last Roman administrator had left, stood before the ruins of Roman Bath, Aquae Sulis, and tried to put into words what they saw.

The poem has come down to us damaged and incomplete, half-eaten by time, missing whole passages. We call it The Ruin. What survives is one of the most quietly devastating things ever written in English.

Wrætlic is þes wealstan, wyrde gebræcon,
burgstede burston, brosnað enta geweorc.
Wondrous is this masonry, broken by fate,
the city-places have crumbled, the work of giants decays.

The poet described roofless halls and fallen towers. The frost on the stones. The place where men had once laughed and drunk and glittered with gold. They described the hot springs still steaming, still running, still warm, three centuries after the last Roman had used them, as though the earth itself remembered what had been built above it and refused to forget.

The poet had no word for Roman. No concept of the empire that had built this, governed this, garrisoned this, taxed this, Christianized this, and then, exhaustedly, bureaucratically, with a letter nobody quite remembers sending, let go of this.

They saw only the evidence of a greatness they could not name, in a language that carried no memory of what had made it. And they wrote it down.

That act, the Anglo-Saxon poet standing in the ruins and recording their wonder at the work of giants, is the strange, melancholy full stop at the end of Roman Britain. Four centuries of roads and walls and law and language and religion, of olive oil from Spain and wine from Gaul and letters home complaining about the cold, reduced in human memory to the evidence of a vanished race of builders.

Rome came to Britain not to liberate it, not to love it, not to stay. It came to extract, to garrison, to tax, and in the end, to leave. What it built in the leaving was something it never intended: a people practiced in surviving without it.

What remained, the roads still running, the walls still standing, the hot springs still steaming, the church still singing in Latin to congregations who no longer spoke it, the genes and place-names and legal habits and crop rotations quietly absorbed into the fabric of an island, was the ghost of an occupation that had lasted longer than the United States has yet existed.

The Anglo-Saxon poet stood in the ruins and marveled at the work of giants.

We are still, in some sense, standing in it.

title.$t: Roman Britannia, Part III: The Wall and the Warlords

content.$t:
Hadrian’s Wall and the Governors Who Wanted to Be Emperor: How Rome solved the problem of Britain- and created a far more dangerous one in doing so.

In 306 CE, a British garrison in York did something that would reshape the world: it made a man named Constantine emperor of Rome. But the story of how that happened begins not in a throne room, but in the ash layer still buried beneath London's streets. From Boudica's ruins to Hadrian's Wall to a North African governor who nearly seized the empire, Part III follows the structural trap Rome built for itself- and could never escape.

Bronze statue of Constantine the Great outside York Minster, close to where the British legions proclaimed him emperor in 306 CE.

In short

  • On 25 July 306 CE, the British legions at York proclaimed Constantine emperor; he went on to Christianize the Roman world.
  • Agricola pushed deep into Caledonia (Scotland) between 77 and 84 CE, but was recalled before he could hold it.
  • Hadrian’s Wall, begun around 122 CE, ran coast to coast. It was built to control movement more than to stop armies.
  • Holding Britain took a large army, and a large army made its governor a possible emperor: Rome’s “British Problem”.
  • In 196–197 CE, the governor Clodius Albinus stripped the Wall to fight for the throne, and lost at Lugdunum.

25 July, 306 CE, Eboracum (York)

The old emperor died at dawn. His name was Constantius, and he had ruled the western empire for a decade with weary competence. He died in a garrison city at the northern edge of the Roman world, in the cold stone fortress the Romans called Eboracum- a city on the Ouse that we now call York.

His son was at the bedside. The troops were already in the courtyard. What happened next took perhaps an hour.

The soldiers- British legions, most of them, men who had spent their careers on the Wall and in the northern forts, men who were loyal to their general and only theoretically loyal to whatever emperor sat in Rome- turned to the dead Emperor’s son, raised him on a shield, and acclaimed him Augustus- Emperor of Rome.

Colossal Portrait of Constantine I, Capitoline Museums. Fragment of a colossal marble statue of Constantine I, c.315–325 CE, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

His name was Flavius Valerius Constantinus- Constantine the Great. From that rainy courtyard in northern England, Constantine would launch a revolution. He legalized Christianity, moved the empire's capital to Constantinople, and reshaped Western civilization for the next seventeen centuries.

That world-altering history began in the mud of York. It culminated in a dangerous, insular pattern: Britain's legions had realized they had the power to make kings.

“To understand why the legions of Britain felt entitled to make an emperor without asking Rome’s permission, you have to understand what Britain had become since Boudica burned three cities to the ground - and what Hadrian’s Wall had accidentally turned it into.”

I. The Roman Britain Rebuilt- Britain After the Ash

Fishbourne Roman Palace mosaic, West Sussex. The dolphin and cupid mosaic at Fishbourne Roman Palace, West Sussex, c.75 CE.

The fire layer is still there. Archaeologists call it the Boudican destruction horizon. Half a meter beneath the modern streets of London lies a permanent band of black, charred earth- the physical residue of the year 61 CE, when Queen Boudica burned Rome’s initial colony to the ground.

It is not an abstraction. It is the physical residue of how close this province came to being lost entirely. But Rome did not lose it.

The governor Suetonius Paulinus crushed Boudica’s force in a single set-piece battle. Then he went on punishing the rebel tribes so thoroughly that his own superiors in Rome grew alarmed. When the new procurator wrote to the emperor complaining that the governor’s scorched-earth policy was destroying the tax base the province existed to provide, Paulinus was recalled.

It was a characteristically Roman response: military victory followed by administrative adjustment. The governor who replaced Paulinus was more conciliatory, and he initiated a more restrained policy. The tribes that had not rebelled were rewarded. The tribes that had rebelled were carefully, deliberately brought back into the provincial economy.

Over the next few decades, southern Britain underwent a dramatic transformation. Londinium was rebuilt grander than before, with a new forum larger than any other north of the Alps, a governor’s palace on the Thames waterfront, and public baths. Camulodunum rose with a new defensive wall- the oldest surviving Roman town wall in Britain, still standing in Colchester today.

In the south, the villas multiplied: mosaic floors, hypocaust heating, olive oil from Spain, wine from Gaul, glassware from Syria. A Briton born in the decade of Boudica’s rebellion could, by old age, look out from a colonnaded townhouse at a landscape so Roman that the torched roundhouses of their childhood might have belonged to a different world entirely.

But that comfortable, Romanized south rested on a foundation that was never fully stable. Because north and west of the new towns and villas, the province had a problem it could not solve by building better roads.

II. The Edge That Would Not Yield - Agricola’s Push North

Gnaeus Julius Agricola arrived as governor of Britain in 77 CE and spent the next seven years doing something no Roman governor had quite managed before: he was patient. He did not simply march north and force a battle. He built roads as he went. He established supply lines. He fortified as he advanced. By the standards of Roman frontier commanders, he was methodical to the point of being unusual.

Agricola’s campaigns in Britain, 78–84 CE. Map of Governor Gnaeus Julius Agricola’s northward advance, 77–84 CE. He reached further into Caledonia than any Roman general before or after him, and was recalled before he could consolidate it. The territory he abandoned would define Rome’s limits in Britain for the next three centuries.

He pacified the remaining tribes of Wales. By 83 CE, he had pushed the legions deep into Scotland's rugged highlands, smashing the Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius.

But a suspicious emperor abruptly recalled Agricola to Rome; the advance stalled, and the far northern frontier devolved into a violent, unpredictable border zone. The northern forts were thinned. The advance stalled. The province contracted. During this volatile period, around 120 CE, the battle-hardened Ninth Legion mysteriously vanished from the historical record.

Hadrian became emperor in 117 CE and arrived in Britain in 122 CE to assess the problem himself. What he found convinced him that the far north could not be held. He decided that the wild Scottish Highlands were not worth the endless cost in Roman blood.

He chose to draw a permanent line in stone. He built a wall that still stands today.

III. Hadrian’s Wall- The Empire Draws Its Line

Hadrian’s Wall, Northumberland. Hadrian’s Wall running west across the Northumberland landscape- 73 Roman miles of stone, begun in 122 CE and taking eight years to complete.

Hadrian’s Wall was begun around 122 CE and took roughly eight years to complete. It ran 73 Roman miles- about 80 modern miles- coast to coast across the narrowest neck of the island.

At its core, it was a wall: up to ten feet wide, originally perhaps fifteen feet high, built from dressed stone quarried from the surrounding landscape.

But the Wall itself was only one layer of a system. In front of it, a wide ditch. Behind it, a military road giving rapid north-south movement. Further south still, a second earthwork barrier called the Vallum marked the limit of the military zone. Every Roman mile, a fortified gateway. Every five to eight miles, a full fort could hold a cohort of five hundred or more soldiers. Observation towers were placed between every milecastle. Signal systems to pass messages coast to coast in minutes.

The Wall was not primarily designed to stop an army. The Wall was designed to control. It controlled who moved, what they carried, where they went, and what they paid in tolls and taxes. Every gate was a checkpoint. The whole system was customs and intelligence infrastructure as much as military fortification- Rome’s administrative logic carved into the northern landscape.

The Wall worked, in the narrow sense: the province south of it was never again overrun, as Boudica had nearly done.

Vindolanda writing tablets, c.85–130 CE. The Vindolanda tablets, British Museum- the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain. Duty rosters, grain inventories, a birthday invitation, a soldier’s request for more socks against the northern cold. The Wall in the soldiers’ own words.

But maintaining it required a massive standing army at the edge of the earth, creating a far more dangerous problem than the architects of Roman Britannia had planned for.

IV. The British Paradox - Why Britain’s Strength Was Its Downfall

Here is the problem at the heart of Roman Britain, the problem that no emperor or governor ever fully solved, the problem that runs from Boudica’s ash to the moment the troops in that York courtyard raised Constantine on a shield.

Britain required a large army to govern. The island was geographically isolated- cut off from the rest of the empire by the Channel, with a permanently restive north that needed constant garrisoning.

A weak military presence meant what it had meant under Boudica: a province that could be overrun from within. Rome needed soldiers here. Lots of them.

But a large army meant a powerful commander. Operating at the end of the longest supply line in the Western world, the Governor of Britain functioned less like a politician and more like an autonomous monarch.

“In normal times, when Rome was stable, and the emperor was strong, and there was no civil war to tempt a general’s ambition, this arrangement functioned. The governor governed. The army garrisoned. The taxes were collected. The Wall was maintained. The times were not always normal.”

V. Albinus- The First March

Marble bust, Severan period, c.193–211 CE. Marble portrait bust from the Severan period, late 2nd to early 3rd century CE.

Roman historians refer to 193 CE as the Year of the Five Emperors.

The emperor Commodus had been strangled on New Year’s Eve of 192 CE. His replacement, Pertinax, lasted eighty-seven days before being murdered by the Praetorian Guard. The Guard then auctioned the office of emperor to the highest bidder. A wealthy senator named Didius Julianus won. He lasted sixty-six days.

Into this chaos stepped three provincial governors, each with a large army and a legitimate claim to have had enough. One was Pescennius Niger in the east. One was Septimius Severus, commander of the Danubian legions. And the other was Decimus Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain.

Albinus was himself a product of Rome's remarkable geographic reach. He was born in Hadrumetum, a prosperous port city on the North African coast in what is now Tunisia, to a Roman family long settled in the province of Africa Proconsularis. He had grown up under the wide skies and warm sun of the Mediterranean world, far removed from the grey northern frontier he would eventually be sent to govern.

He had served in military posts across the empire before receiving Britain, and he was known, unusually for a frontier commander, as a man of literary cultivation. The Historia Augusta credits him with writing pastoral fables in his spare time. Whether the cold rain of Britannia suited a man from the warmth of North Africa is not recorded. What is clear is that he understood the province he inherited, and he governed it, for the first years, with efficiency and genuine care.

Civil war erupted in Rome. Albinus was not a fool. He recognized that he could not fight both Niger and Severus simultaneously. When Severus offered him the title of Caesar, junior emperor, Albinus accepted.

Coin of Clodius Albinus, c.193–197 CE. Aureus of Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain, struck c.193–197 CE. Born in Hadrumetum, North Africa, he governed Britain with competence and loyalty- until the moment he had to choose between obedience and the throne.

It was a trap. By 196 CE, Severus had eliminated his eastern rivals and turned his sights on Britain. Knowing his life was forfeit, Albinus made his move. He crossed the Channel to claim the supreme title of Augustus.

This bought Albinus time; he stabilized Britain and kept his options open while Severus disposed of Niger in the east. By 196 CE, with Niger defeated, it was clear that Severus had no intention of honoring the arrangement.

Albinus made his move. To win a continental war, Albinus made the catastrophic decision to strip the island bare. Forts along Hadrian’s Wall were abandoned, and the entire permanent garrison of Britain was ferried to Gaul.

By early 197 CE, Albinus controlled Gaul, Spain, and Britain. Severus marched west to meet him. The armies of Albinus and Severus collided in one of the bloodiest conflicts in Roman history at Lugdunum, modern Lyon, on 19 February 197 CE. It was one of the largest battles fought on Western European soil since the Republic's fall. Over 150,000 Roman citizens slaughtered each other.

Albinus’s British legions fought with ferocious bravery, nearly breaking Severus’s lines, but a decisive cavalry charge broke the British flank. Albinus’s army was systematically butchered. Defeated, the British governor fled to a nearby house and fell on his sword.

The British army that had followed him was decimated. The province that had produced him was stripped of soldiers, left exposed on its northern frontier, and governed for the next generation by men chosen for their loyalty rather than their competence.

VI. The Legacy of the Flame

Victorian commemorative mural, Governors of Roman Britain. A Victorian-era mural depicting the great governors and figures of Roman Britain: Septimius Severus, Antoninus Pius, Hadrian, Agricola, and Tacitus.

Back on the lonely northern frontier of Britannia, Albinus’s ambition was paid for in ash. The native tribes realized the Wall was empty. They poured south across the undefended border, leaving a stark archaeological layer of burning, looting, and destruction across the northern forts. Rome took years to rebuild the line.

In 208 CE, the aging, gout-ridden Emperor Septimius Severus personally traveled to Britain to crush the northern tribes. He launched brutal, exhausting scorched-earth campaigns into Scotland, but the relentless guerrilla warfare broke his remaining health.

He withdrew south to the military headquarters at Eboracum and died within the stone walls of York in 211 CE.

The template of Roman Britannia was set. The island was no longer just a difficult frontier. Britain was not just a difficult province to govern. It was a province that, in moments of Roman weakness, would act. Albinus had proven that the governor of Britain- with his wall, his isolated legions, and his island kingdom- could look at a fractured empire and make a credible play for the throne of the world.

This was what Roman called the British Problem. The governors were warlords of an island kingdom. And warlords, when the throne of the world becomes available, have a habit of reaching for it.

Albinus was the first. He would not be the last.

Others would notice. A century later, in that very same city of York, Constantine would succeed.


                            At a glance: where Part III sits in four centuries of Roman Britain.

Magnus Maximus, Constantine’s acclamation, the legions’ last departure - and the question of what, exactly, was left behind.

How a stuttering scholar-emperor finished what Caesar couldn’t- and what happened to an island that refused to stay conquered. The story of war elephants and Boudica's rebellion.

Claudius, a War Elephant and Boudica: How Rome Conquered Britain with a Stammering Emperor

I. The Lucanian Ox

Hannibal Barca crossing the Alps with his war elephants, 218 BCE- the terror Rome never forgot.

In short

  • Rome learned the terror of a weapon it had no name for from Hannibal’s elephants, and used that lesson in Britain 250 years later.
  • Claudius, mocked as a stammering fool, sent four legions under Aulus Plautius to invade Britain in 43 CE.
  • He spent just sixteen days on the island and brought a war elephant to the Thames; eleven British kings submitted.
  • Londinium grew from a Thames marsh into the province’s commercial heart, tied together by straight Roman roads.
  • In 60 or 61 CE, Boudica of the Iceni burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before Rome crushed her army.

His name was Hannibal Barca, and he was twenty-nine years old when he set out to destroy Rome. In the autumn of 218 BCE, he assembled an army at Cartagena on the Spanish coast: roughly 90,000 infantry, 12,000 cavalry, and 37 war elephants.

He then marched them east across the Pyrenees, through the hostile tribes of southern Gaul, and up into the Alps as the first snows of winter fell. The Romans, expecting any Carthaginian threat to arrive by sea, simply could not believe what their scouts were reporting. Nobody crossed the Alps in winter. Nobody crossed the Alps at all with an army that size. It was logistically impossible and tactically insane.

Hannibal did it in fifteen days.

Rome, completely unprepared for an enemy already inside Italy, scrambled to respond. What followed across the next two years was a series of catastrophic Roman defeats- at the Ticinus River, at the Trebia, at Lake Trasimene- that shocked a republic which had never truly known what it was to lose on its own soil.

But at the Trebia, in the bitter December of 218 BCE, the Romans encountered something that would haunt their military thinking for generations. From somewhere in the river mist on Hannibal’s flank, something came towards the Roman soldiers that they had no name for. The Roman soldiers who waded across the freezing Trebia that morning had heard reports of the great beasts. None of them had ever seen one. They had a name borrowed from the Greek- elephas- but many of the ordinary legionaries simply called them Lucanian oxen. The word elephant meant almost nothing to a soldier from a Roman farming family. An ox from Lucania, he could at least picture.

What came at him across the battlefield was nothing like an ox.

Each animal stood twice the height of a man at the shoulder. They carried towers strapped to their backs, with archers and javelin-throwers. They screamed- a sound no Roman had a frame of reference for, something between a trumpet and a living roar that carried across the whole field. The Roman cavalry horses, who had trained against every weapon a human enemy could produce, simply broke. They could not be held. They turned and bolted, carrying their riders with them, and that collapse of the flanks opened the Roman lines to Hannibal’s infantry like a blade opening a seam.

Rome lost thousands that day. It would lose tens of thousands more before it turned the tide. But it learned. Roman armies began training their horses to elephants, began developing tactics to split and encircle them, began understanding that the animals, for all their terror, were also vulnerable- to fire, to pain, to the panic of their own side if turned by wounds. The creature that had once seemed like a supernatural weapon became, in time, just another problem to be solved.

Rome solved it. Rome always solved it eventually.

But from that frozen morning on, Rome never forgot the lesson: that there is no terror quite like facing a weapon you have no name for. That the unknown, when unleashed, can break a line that swords and spears never could.

Two and a half centuries later, it would use it.

II. The Stammering Emperor and the Unfinished Island

The Emperor Claudius- dragged from behind a curtain and declared emperor. He repaid his rescuers with a continent.

In the winter of 41 CE, the Praetorian Guard dragged a terrified man out from behind a curtain in the imperial palace- where he had been hiding in genuine fear for his life during the chaos following Caligula’s assassination- and declared him Emperor of Rome.

His name was Claudius. He was fifty years old; he walked with a limp, and he stuttered so badly that he avoided public speaking whenever he could. His grandmother, Livia, described him as someone nature had left unfinished. His mother Antonia called him a monster and used his name as her personal shorthand for stupidity. For decades the Roman political class had kept him at a careful distance- harmless, they agreed, because he was so clearly not a threat to anyone.

None of them had noticed that Claudius had spent those decades becoming perhaps the most learned man in Rome. He understood something Caligula, with all his divine pretensions, had not: that an emperor’s authority rested on a foundation of military prestige- and that his own foundation was dangerously thin.

He needed a conquest. He needed it to be undeniable. He looked north, across the Channel, at the one conspicuous piece of unfinished business in the western empire- the island that had made Caesar look incomplete and Caligula look absurd, sitting just twenty-one miles from the coast of Gaul, visible on a clear day, yet unconquered and unRoman.

Not for much longer.

The Roman invasion of Britain, 43 CE- four legions, a general, and a deliberate pause on the Thames.

In the spring of 43 CE, four battle-hardened legions assembled on the Gallic coast- the Second Augusta, the Ninth Hispana, the Fourteenth Gemina, and the Twentieth Valeria Victrix. Under the steady command of Aulus Plautius, they crossed the Channel, waded ashore in Kent, fought through the marshes, and faced a coalition of British tribes in a brutal two-day battle at the Medway that shattered local resistance. They pushed to the Thames- and then stopped. And waited.

They were waiting for the emperor.

Claudius crossed to Britain for exactly sixteen days. He brought reinforcements, Praetorian guardsmen, and, shipped across the Channel in specially constructed transport vessels, a fully armored war elephant. The Britons standing on the northern bank of the Thames had never seen an elephant in their lives. They had no word for what they were looking at- no story, no warning, nothing in the whole of their island’s memory that came close to preparing them for the sight of that animal emerging from the river mist, the ground shaking under its feet, its scream cutting through the autumn air like nothing they had ever heard.

Any thought of resistance died on the spot. Eleven British kings surrendered on the bank of the Thames that day without a further blow being struck. The age of the blue-painted warrior was ending. The age of the stone city was about to begin.

III. The Surrender- and the North That Didn’t

The collapse of the southern tribes was swift and, by Roman standards, relatively clean. Kings who bent the knee could keep their titles, their lands, and a measure of their dignity, provided they paid their taxes, cooperated with Roman administration, and didn't cause trouble. Rome was practical about these things. Outright submission was always preferable to prolonged resistance, which was expensive, bloody, and inconvenient for everyone.

But as the legions pushed farther north and west, Rome's “civilizing” mission hit a wall of geological and human resistance. The further they marched from the flat, fertile south, the harder the land became- and the harder the people with it.

In what the Romans called Caledonia- the territory we now know as Scotland- the landscape dissolved into jagged heaths and dark lochs that swallowed Roman formations whole. The northern tribes waged a brand of guerrilla warfare that made the disciplined Roman legion, designed for open-field battle, look slow and cumbersome. They hit and vanished. They burned what they could not hold. They refused to behave like an enemy Rome knew how to defeat.

The Romans did the math and found it didn't add up. The cost in men and treasure of occupying the far north far outweighed anything the territory could return in taxes or resources. The decision was quietly made to settle on a boundary- and south of that boundary, to build.

Inside the new province of Britannia, however, the blue-stained ghosts of the forest had not finished with Rome yet.

IV. Londinium- The City on the Marsh

Reconstruction of Londinium, c.120 CE- from a mudflat on the Thames to the commercial heart of the entire province.

Once the Roman boot was firmly planted, the transformation of the British landscape was nothing short of extraordinary. The Romans practiced what historians have called the religion of urbanism- a deep, almost theological conviction that true civilization could only exist within the structured walls of a stone city. The roundhouse, the hill fort, the sacred grove: these were not civilisation. They were its absence. And Rome set about filling that absence with breathtaking speed.

Nowhere was this more visible than in a small, marshy settlement on the northern bank of the Thames, where the river was narrow enough to bridge and deep enough for ocean-going vessels. The Romans called it Londinium. Within a generation it would become the beating commercial heart of the entire province- a glittering metropolis of marble, tile, and brick rising from a mudflat.

Roads came first- always roads. The Romans understood that a province you cannot move through quickly is a province you cannot hold. They drove straight, paved roads across the island with an engineer’s indifference to the landscape, connecting their new towns and military forts in a web of stone that Britain would still travel along two thousand years later. Along these roads flowed soldiers, tax collectors, merchants, and goods from across the known world.

By the second century, a Briton could walk down a paved street in Londinium and buy olive oil from Spain, wine from Gaul, and pepper that had traveled thousands of miles from the Indian coast. They could visit stone theatres, conduct business in colonnaded forums, and soak in vast public baths where hot water ran from carved fountains.

Beneath the floors of the wealthier houses ran a system the Romans called a hypocaust- channels of warm air pumped from a furnace below, keeping the stone floors heated through the brutal British winter. For a people who had spent thousands of years in timber-and-mud roundhouses, huddled against the cold, this was not merely comfort. It was a different conception of what human life could be.

V. Taxation, Subjugation, and the Slow Transformation

But comfort and subjugation often arrive in the same package.

The Roman administration expected the province to pay for itself- and pay for it, it did. Taxes were levied on land, on trade, on inheritance. Roman officials- not always scrupulous, not always fair- managed the collection with an efficiency that the tribal Britons had never experienced and did not always find agreeable. Land that had belonged to a tribe for generations was assessed, valued, and taxed. Chiefs who had once commanded loyalty through warfare and generosity now had to navigate a bureaucratic system designed in a city a thousand miles away by men who had never seen their island.

The pressure to Romanize was not always violent. Often it was subtler and, in many ways, more corrosive- the draining away of the old ways not through conquest but through replacement.

The Druids, the intellectual and spiritual backbone of British tribal society, were systematically suppressed. Their sacred groves were burned. Their oral traditions, never written down, began to fade. Latin crept into commerce, administration, and the mouths of children of collaborating aristocrats who sent their sons to Roman schools and watched them come back wearing togas.

Some Britons prospered enormously under Rome. They built townhouses with mosaic floors, traded in the new economy, and became, in all the ways that mattered administratively, Roman. Others watched from the edges- tribes dispossessed of their land, families taxed into destitution, kings stripped of real power while being permitted the hollow theatre of their titles- and they seethed quietly.

Seventeen years after the invasion, the seething caught fire.

VI. Boudica- The Fire Queen

Boadicea and Her Daughters- bronze by Thomas Thornycroft, erected at Westminster Bridge, 1902.

Her name was Boudica, queen of the Iceni tribe of what is now Norfolk, and she did not begin as Rome’s enemy. Her husband Prasutagus had been a client king- one of those cooperative rulers who bent the knee, paid his taxes, and was permitted to govern in name while Rome governed in practice. When he died, he left his kingdom jointly to his two daughters and to the Roman Emperor, a diplomatic arrangement designed to protect his family’s position.

Rome ignored it entirely. Imperial officials seized the Iceni lands as if they were simply conquered territory, flogged Boudica publicly, and assaulted her daughters. It was not just cruelty. It was a catastrophic political miscalculation.

Boudica united the tribes- the Iceni, the Trinovantes, and others nursing their own grievances- and turned them into an army. Ancient sources describe her as tall and terrifying, with a great mass of red hair that fell to her waist and a voice like a crack of thunder that could command thousands into silence. She led her coalition south with a fury that the Romans, spread thin across the province, were wholly unprepared for.

Camulodunum- modern Colchester, the first Roman capital of Britain- fell first and burned to the ground. A relief force of Roman infantry was destroyed almost to the last man. Then Londinium, which had no walls and no garrison capable of defending it, the Roman governor abandoned and left to its fate. Boudica’s army entered the city and burned it so completely that archaeologists today still find, several meters below the streets of modern London, a distinct layer of dark red ash- the physical scar of a single afternoon in 60 or 61 CE.

Verulamium- modern St Albans- burned next. By the time the Roman governor Gaius Paulinus wheeled his legions around and brought Boudica to battle- choosing his ground carefully, a narrow defile that neutralized her numerical advantage- somewhere between seventy and eighty thousand people were dead across the three cities.

Relief from Trajan’s Column, Rome- the methodical Roman testudo, the shield wall that waited for Boudica’s charge.

The battle itself was methodical. The Romans held their ground, waited for the charge to exhaust itself against their lines, and then pushed forward with the cold precision of men who had been doing this for centuries. Boudica’s army, crammed in by its own wagons at the rear, could not retreat. The slaughter was immense.

Boudica herself died shortly after- by her own hand, according to some sources, by illness according to others. She left no grave that anyone has ever found, no monument, no marked place of burial. She simply vanished from the record, as suddenly and completely as she had erupted into it.

But she left something behind. She left that layer of ash under London. She left the memory of what a province pushed too hard could do. And she left, simmering in the island’s northern and western edges, a question Rome would spend the next three centuries trying to answer:

How do you hold a people who have already decided, in their bones, that they will not be held?

That question- and the extraordinary answer Rome attempted to build in stone across the width of the island- is where our next part begins.


At a glance: where Part II sits in four centuries of Roman Britain.

The empire draws a line, and everything south of it starts to crack.

title.$t: Roman Britannia, Part I: The Work of Giants

content.$t:
How an island of stone circles and blue-painted warriors first felt the Roman Eagle.

Before Rome Conquered Britain: Stonehenge, Caesar and Caligula’s Seashells


If you have ever watched the television series Vikings, you may remember a quiet scene in which the monk Athelstan and King Ecbert of Wessex stand together in the shadow of old Roman ruins. Looking up at the massive stone arches, Ecbert asks how any human hand could have shaped something so perfect.

Athelstan answers that his people call these ruins the enta geweorc- the “work of giants”. This phrase in Old English says it all.

“And did they?” Ecbert presses. “Were they giants, Athelstan?”

“No,” the monk replies. “They were men like us, Ecbert. But they were men who did not have to look to their own defenses every time the moon waxed full. Their hearts were beating for a city a thousand miles away that had already forgotten them, and that was their undoing.”

“If they were men, then the knowledge is not magic,” Ecbert says. “It is merely lost.”

“It is a paradox,” Athelstan whispers. “They built the most formidable fortress in the world, and then they abandoned it to chase a crown they could not hold. They left us their stones, but they took the light with them. Now we are scavengers in a graveyard of giants, trying to remember how to be men again.”

In short

  • Rome ruled Britain for nearly 400 years, from 43 to 410 CE. Centuries later, the Saxons called the ruins enta geweorc, “the work of giants”.
  • Britain became an island around 6,000 BCE, when rising seas drowned Doggerland. Stonehenge went up in stages from about 3,000 BCE.
  • The Iron Age Britons, guided by their Druids, went to war with lime-washed hair, gold torcs and bodies stained blue with woad.
  • Julius Caesar landed twice, in 55 and 54 BCE, and left both times without conquering the island.
  • In 40 CE Caligula massed an army on the Channel, then had his soldiers gather seashells as “the spoils of the sea”.

The Roman Eagle ruled these islands for nearly four hundred years, from roughly 43 to 410 CE. By the time Ecbert became Saxon king of Wessex, the occupation of Britain was so far in the past that ordinary people could no longer believe a human hand had laid those stones. To the Saxons, farmers who lived in simple wooden huts, Roman engineering was so advanced that it looked like the work of a vanished race of titans.

For Ecbert, who would unite much of England four centuries after the fall of Roman Britannia, the ruins were more than crumbling masonry. He did not see arches; he saw a blueprint- a record of how an empire had once controlled every inch of this land through organization and engineering that his own people could no longer replicate.

This “work of giants” sets the stage for our journey: an island forcibly turned into an imperial jewel and then left to rot until the locals could no longer read the walls they lived among. But to understand the story of Roman Britannia, we must first look past the Eagle, into the island’s true prehistory.

I. The Neolithic Northerners- Builders of Stonehenge

Stonehenge, Wiltshire- built in stages from c.3000 BCE, aligned to the solstices, a calendar in stone.

Long before the first Roman legionary set foot on its shores, Britain was a land of deep primeval forests and chalky highlands. By the late Iron Age it was home to the painted warriors the Romans dreaded- the same, blue-stained tribesmen who had been raiding into Gaul for generations. But the human story of these islands begins thousands of years earlier.

People first drifted north as the glaciers retreated, around 12,000 BCE. Britain was not yet an island. For the next six millennia it remained a peninsula of Europe, joined to the continent by a vast, low-lying land bridge known to modern archaeologists as Doggerland.

Around 6,000 BCE, rising seas finally drowned that bridge, severing the inhabitants from the mainland and erasing the English Channel from memory. The people left behind were a hardy mix of hunter-gatherers. In time, the first Neolithic farmers arrived in small boats, bringing wheat, cattle, and a knowledge of the seasons. They were deeply attuned to the cycles of the earth, surviving brutal northern winters through grit and communal labor.

They did not just inhabit the land; they marked it. They dragged stones the size of barns across hundreds of miles to raise monuments that still defy easy explanation. The most famous is Stonehenge, built in stages from around 3,000 BCE. The alignment of its trilithons with the midwinter and midsummer solstices reveals an advanced grasp of the heavens- a calendar in stone for a people whose lives were dictated by the turning of the year. What ultimately happened to these Neolithic builders remains one of prehistory’s great open questions.

II. The Painted Isle- Ancient Britons of the Iron Age

A reconstruction of an Iron Age Celtic warrior: lime-washed hair, golden torc, body stained with woad.

By the time the Iron Age Britons inherited this land, the megaliths were already holy mysteries- silent stones that had stood for thousands of years. These ancient Britons were a hardy, tribal people who outlasted the island’s brutal winters in timber-and-mud roundhouses. Led by the Druids, who served as their judges, scholars, and priests, they lived in fortified hilltop settlements and were legendary for their terrifying appearance in battle: tall, lime-washed hair, gold torcs at the throat, and bodies stained blue with woad.

Long before the Roman Eagle saw them face to face, the people of Gaul and mainland Europe had been trading stories about the island and its inhabitants since the early Bronze Age- its tin mines, its brilliant pottery, it’s strange priests who held the power of life and death in the sacred groves. Soon this wild, blue-stained world would collide with the most efficient war machine the ancient world had ever produced.

III. Julius Caesar and the First Roman Encounters (55–54 BCE)

Roman soldiers fighting their way ashore, carved in relief. Caesar’s legions met the Britons in the surf.

The shadow of the Roman Eagle first reached for the island in 55 BCE, driven by the ambition of Julius Caesar. Fresh from his bloody campaigns in Gaul, Caesar viewed Britain as more than a legendary mystery. It was a strategic nuisance: the British tribes were quietly sheltering and reinforcing their Gallic cousins, and Caesar meant to sever that lifeline- while burnishing his own glory in the process.

His first expedition was a logistical nightmare. The English Channel, with its terrifying surges and unpredictable tides, nearly swallowed his fleet before it could even land. When the Roman legionaries finally reached the shore, they were met by a sight that would haunt their nightmares: thousands of blue-stained warriors, screaming and waiting for them in the surf. Caesar carved out a temporary foothold but was quickly humbled when a North Sea storm smashed his anchored ships at their moorings. He limped back to the mainland with little more than a handful of hostages and a bruised ego.

Undeterred, and desperate to erase the embarrassment, he returned a year later in 54 BCE with a force the world had never seen cross those waters: eight hundred ships and five veteran legions. This time he pushed inland, crossed the Thames, and forced the powerful tribal leader Cassivellaunus to sue for peace. It was a tactical victory and a strategic failure. Caesar exacted promises of tribute and built thin diplomatic ties, but brewing instability back in Rome and a massive revolt in Gaul forced him to withdraw every last soldier. Britain slipped out of his hands as cleanly as it had slipped in.

Eight hundred ships, five veteran legions- and still Britain refused to stay conquered. Caesar’s campaigns were a reminder that the Channel was not a river to be crossed; it was a moat around a world of its own.

❦

IV. The Century of Silence, and Caligula’s Seashells (54 BCE–40 CE)

The Emperor Caligula- the man who declared war on the ocean, and whose seashells nearly became Rome’s most embarrassing trophy.

Britain remained an unconquered “client kingdom” in all but name for the next century. During this long century of silence, the Emperor Augustus planned several invasions, each one quietly cancelled before a single ship was launched. Augustus learned what Caesar had only suspected: the Channel was a moat, and Britain was a problem easier to admire from a distance.

Then came the strangest chapter in the whole prologue, and it belonged to the Emperor Caligula.

Volatile, eccentric, and by every contemporary account half-mad, Caligula could have annexed Britannia if he had simply been a more stable man. In 40 CE he amassed a colossal force on the coast of Gaul- by some accounts as many as two hundred thousand troops, drawn up in full view of the Channel and seemingly prepared to finish what Caesar had started a century earlier.

To grasp what happened on that beach, you have to understand what kind of emperor was standing on it. Even by the brutal standards of Roman power, Caligula’s reputation was something apart. He had taken the throne in 37 CE as a popular young prince, the son of the beloved general Germanicus, and for a few months Rome adored him. Then, barely six months into his reign, a serious illness nearly killed him. By every ancient account, the man who climbed out of that sickbed was not the one who had climbed in.

What followed was a four-year carnival of cruelty and self-deification. He forced his teenage cousin and co-heir, Tiberius Gemellus, to suicide. He exiled his own sisters on charges of treason. He demanded to be worshipped as a living god in his own lifetime, ordered his statue erected inside the Temple in Jerusalem, touching off a near-revolt across Judea. He is said to have appointed his favorite horse, Incitatus, a priest of his own cult. Suetonius records his favourite line, lifted from an old tragedy and aimed at his terrified senators:

“Oderint dum metuant. Let them hate me, so long as they fear me.”

Within months of the beach at the Channel, his own Praetorian Guard would cut him down in a palace corridor. So, it is against this backdrop- a god-emperor who picked fights with the sea, the senate, and his own family- that we have to read what happened next on the shore of the ocean.

Then, at the water’s edge, something inside him snapped.

In one of the most bizarre displays in military history, Caligula reportedly lost his nerve as he stared across the Channel. Instead of boarding the ships, he commanded his confused legions to charge the waves with their swords drawn, and then to fill their helmets with seashells. These shells, he announced, were the spoils of his conquered ocean. He had the trophies displayed in Rome.

“Spolia oceani. The spoils of the conquered sea.”

The invasion was aborted. The legions went home bewildered, the senators went home embarrassed, and Caligula went home to be murdered within the year. But the months of troop-massing on the Gallic shore had done one thing his sanity could not: they had built a psychological bridge across the water. The next emperor who looked north would no longer be able to pretend the island wasn’t there.

The empire would come for Britain at last, but it would not be the man who stared down the Channel who brought it. That story belongs to a stammering, mocked outsider; to four battle-hardened legions wading through the marshes of Kent; and to a creature no Briton on the island had ever seen in his life.

But that is a tale for the next part.


                                                At a glance: where Part I sits in four centuries of Roman Britain.

Next: Roman Britannia Part II: The Birth of Roman Britannia
How a stuttering scholar-emperor finished what Caesar couldn’t- and what happened to an island that refused to stay conquered.

This article was first published on Substack on May 19, 2026, as Part I of the four-part series The Story of Roman Britannia.
