title.$t: The Mysterious Life of the Eel

content.$t:
Guests of the River, Children of the Sea

That eel in a muddy monsoon field was born in the Indian Ocean, and it’s going back there to die. No one has ever seen where.

The eel that suddenly appears in muddy monsoon fields is not native to the region. Its astonishing life cycle, born in the sea, raised in rivers, and returning to the ocean to breed, has puzzled scientists from Aristotle’s time to the present.

This article was first published in Nepali in Onlinekhabar’s on July 31, 2026 (Saun 15, 2083 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: onlinekhabar.com ↗

Born in the sea, raised in rivers: the eel’s life cycle at a glance.

Many of us assume the eels (bam) we find in muddy fields during the monsoon rains are native here, like hile, buhari, and other fish. I too learned only much later that the eels found in Nepal are born in the Indian Ocean, spend a few decades in our fields and streams, and return to the very place they were born to have their young.

How freshwater eels reproduce is something we have only recently begun to understand, based on limited evidence and educated guesses. No one yet knows for certain where in the Indian Ocean, across the Bay of Bengal, Nepal’s eels come from. In fact, no one has ever directly observed eels spawning, that is, releasing their eggs and sperm, nor has anyone managed to capture it on camera.

Aristotle’s Mistake and Freud’s Search

Curiosity about how eels are born is nothing new. As far as we know, Aristotle was the first person to investigate it.

Many of us know that a female fish lays eggs, that an embryo forms when a male’s sperm fertilizes them, and that a new fish is born from it. But this is exactly where eels differ from other fish.

Almost all fish have markers that distinguish males from females. In these species, males develop testes and females develop ovaries. But in freshwater eels, the reproductive organs are not fully developed. So, the question arises: if males and females cannot even be told apart, how are eels born?

Some 2,300 years ago, Aristotle asked this very question. No sperm, no eggs, no reproductive organs like those of other fish. Then how do eels suddenly appear every year in fields, streams, ponds, and ditches with no direct connection to the sea?

Eels were found throughout Europe at the time. Aristotle cut open hundreds of them yet could not find any male or female reproductive organs. Having failed despite every effort, he concluded that eels are born spontaneously from mud.

The belief Aristotle established, that eels are born from mud, persisted for a very long time. In 1876, the world-famous psychoanalyst Sigmund Freud had finished school and enrolled to study medicine. During his studies at a research station in Italy, his first research project was an attempt to locate the eel’s testes. Freud wrote in his memoir that after dissecting nearly four hundred eels without finding testes, he turned to the study of the brain.

Today, Aristotle’s claim that eels are born from mud may make us laugh. It may seem absurd now, but for a long time no one had an answer. Because the freshwater eels Aristotle and Freud examined had not yet developed their reproductive organs, Aristotle and Freud could not find them.

Eels are born in the sea. The tiny young set out on a long journey in search of fresh water, changing form along the way, and live out their adult lives once they reach rivers and streams.

While eels live in freshwater away from the sea, their reproductive organs are not fully developed. Only decades later, when it is time to return to the sea where they were born, do these organs begin to develop.

That is why the mystery of how eels are born persisted for two thousand years after Aristotle. The answer was not in the river; it lay hidden in the distant sea. To put it more plainly, even today no one knows exactly how eels reproduce in the sea.

The answer was not in the river; it lay hidden in the distant sea.

Not a Snake, but a True Fish

When I first saw an eel, it looked to me like a cousin of the rat snake: a long, slippery body, no legs, and a smooth, flowing way of moving through water. Neither was venomous, but there was a world of difference between an eel and a snake.

A snake is a reptile. It breathes with lungs, has dry, scaly skin, and even in water it lives on air. Though it may look like a snake in the water, the eel is not a snake but a true fish of the family Anguillidae.

The eel has every hallmark of a fish: jaws, bones, and gills for breathing underwater. A single fin runs in one continuous line from its back, around the tail, to the underside of its body. That fin helps it swim by twisting its body in waves. Like other fish, the eel breathes through its gills underwater. Its skin, however, is rather special.

Although eels have still not been observed spawning, the available evidence points to one conclusion: adult eels swim thousands of kilometers to reach the Sargasso. One night, at depths of roughly 400 to 1,000 meters, they release their eggs and sperm and then die.

Beneath an eel’s skin lie tiny scales, covered by a slippery coat of slime, or mucus. This mucus keeps the skin slick and moist and allows the eel to absorb some oxygen through the skin itself. That is why an eel can survive out of water somewhat longer than other fish.

Slithering like a snake over damp grass or soil, it can travel from one body of water to another. During a drought, it can survive in a dormant state, buried in mud. This is the secret behind eels ‘suddenly’ appearing after the monsoon rains in fields and ponds that had no water before. They did not fall from the sky; they made their own way there across damp ground.

The eel hunts at night, grows slowly, and rarely draws anyone’s attention. It spends most of its life, sometimes as long as 70–80 years, in our streams, lakes, and wetlands. Seeing this, we assume it is a permanent resident of our rivers and streams.

But in truth, eels are only temporary residents in our fields and streams. To bring a new generation into the world, they must return to the same sea.

In truth, eels are only temporary guests in our fields and streams.

The Final Journey and the Body’s Astonishing Changes

After years in fresh water, one day the eel’s body begins to prepare for its final journey.

Its yellowish-brown skin turns a shiny silver, helping it hide in the deep waters of the sea. It is not only the skin that changes; the body begins to change from within. The eyes swell to nearly twice their size because it must now spend the rest of its life in the deep darkness of the sea. The fins grow broader for long-distance swimming, and the snout becomes pointed.

The most astonishing change occurs in the eel’s digestive system. Its stomach stops working, and its gut begins to waste away. Once it sets out for the sea, it never eats again. The fat it stored over years in streams and rivers becomes its only fuel.

Its reproductive organs develop during the journey to the sea. The eel’s entire body is now shaped for a single purpose: to complete that one-way journey from which it will never return.

This is where the eel’s story gets even stranger. One night, it quietly slips down the stream, through the river and past the estuary toward the open sea. But the eel does not simply head ‘toward the sea.’ It sets off in search of one particular place, where millions of eels from around the world arrive: the place it left as a larva, which it never once reached in all its adult life.

The Atlantic Eel’s Birthplace: The Sargasso Sea

According to scientists, eels originated about 50 million years ago in the Pacific Ocean near what is now Indonesia. Since ancient times, eels’ ancestors have been fish that lived in the deep sea.

At first, they were entirely marine fish. Their larvae drifted far and wide on ocean currents. Over time, some eels extended their journeys even further and, because food was plentiful in freshwater, grew accustomed to reaching it and maturing there.

As eels that originated around Indonesia gradually spread into other seas, new species split off. Today, about 16 eel species are recognized. The European eel (Anguilla anguilla), which Aristotle and Freud studied, belongs to the Atlantic group.

The Atlantic eels have a specific place where they are born and to which they return to spawn: the Sargasso Sea.

An eel leaving a European river must swim five to six thousand kilometers, a months-long journey, to reach its destination. It does so without eating, hiding in the depths by day and rising toward the surface at night. Burning the fat, it has stored all its life, it sets out on this one-way journey. After reaching its destination and spawning, it vanishes forever.

Now the biggest question arises: why do eels from Europe and America make such a long, grueling journey back to the same place, again and again?

Interestingly, American and European eels diverged from each other only about 3 to 6 million years ago. In other words, they evolved into separate species long after the Sargasso current system had formed.

The Sargasso Sea, in the Atlantic Ocean near Bermuda, is one of the strangest seas on Earth. Every other sea has some kind of shore, and countries lay claim to parts of it. But the Sargasso Sea has no shore made of land, and no landmass surrounds it. Its boundaries are set by ocean currents.

The winds near the equator blow one way, while those in the middle latitudes blow the other. This pairing of water and wind turns the waters of the Atlantic into a slow whirl that keeps rotating clockwise.

At the center of this ‘gyre,’ a giant whirl of water, the water collects and remains still. That warm, calm, still center is the Sargasso Sea.

Spread over an area nearly six times the size of France, the sea’s surface is covered with a floating golden seaweed called sargassum. The sea takes its name from this seaweed. Because few nutrients rise from the ocean floor to the surface, there are relatively few other creatures or predators here besides the sargassum.

Spawning at Sea, See-Through Larvae and the Journey to the Rivers

These features are why the Sargasso Sea became the birthplace of Atlantic eels. Its water is warm and calm, providing a place where larvae can escape predators, and the surrounding currents carry them toward the coasts.

The eel’s ancestors had settled into this way of spawning at sea long before they ever encountered rivers. More interesting still, this area was the eels’ breeding ground long before Europe and America were as far apart as they are today.

On a dark night, adult eels release millions of eggs and sperm into the deep waters of the Sargasso. The larvae that hatch look nothing like adult eels. They are five to ten millimeters long, transparent as glass and flat as a leaf. Scientists call them leptocephali (leptocephalus).

Because of its strange shape, the leptocephalus was long thought to be just a kind of sea worm. Scientists discovered only toward the end of the nineteenth century that it is the eel’s larval stage.

More interesting still, these larvae are not built to swim long distances on their own. Thanks to their leaf-like, jellyfish-light bodies, they float easily in the water. Their transparency also helps them evade predators’ eyes.

After leaving the Sargasso, the leptocephali drift with the Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic’s great ocean current. For European eel larvae, this drift can last from one to three years. Along the way, they cover thousands of kilometers.

Along the way, they feed on ‘marine snow.’ On this alone, larvae that were five to ten millimeters long in the Sargasso grow to 60 to 90 millimeters by the time they reach Europe.

After months or years of drifting, the larvae arrive in shallow coastal waters. There, they change form again and become ‘glass eels’: transparent as glass yet shaped like eels.

These glass eels gather at river mouths. Then, riding the tides and guided by Earth’s magnetic field, they head upstream into the rivers. Once they enter freshwater, their bodies begin to take on color, and they become ‘elvers.’ These elvers slowly grow into the yellow eels we see in streams and ponds.

Interestingly, American and European eels diverged from each other only about 3 to 6 million years ago. In other words, they evolved into separate species long after the Sargasso current system had formed.

Tens of millions of years ago, the Atlantic Ocean was much narrower than it is today. Europe and America were also much closer together. As the continents drifted apart, the seafloor spread, and eels began entering rivers in search of food. Yet they never abandoned their ancestral breeding grounds.

So it can be said: the river is a habit they picked up later; the Sargasso is their ancestral home, one they never truly left.

The river is a habit they picked up later; the Sargasso is their ancestral home; one they never truly left.

Born in the middle of the sea thousands of kilometers away, the transparent larvae drift on ocean currents for years until they finally reach a stream on a European or American coast. Then they spend decades in freshwater and grow into adults.

How Do They Find Their Way in the Middle of the Ocean?

The adult eel’s life cycle is complete only when it returns to the same place in the sea to spawn. And here is another marvel: how do they find their way across the open sea to the place where they were born? How do they retain the memory of that place after decades in freshwater? How do Atlantic eels swim thousands of kilometers to find the Sargasso Sea, which has no shore or landmark?

The likely answer lies in the Earth’s magnetic field. The magnetic signature of the waters around the Sargasso Sea may be imprinted in the eel’s brain during its youth. As adults, they navigate using that biological memory.

The European eel’s body works like a compass. By reading the Earth’s magnetic field like a map, eels can head toward the Sargasso’s magnetic signature. A 2017 laboratory study that recreated different magnetic conditions also pointed to this possibility.

Even so, the mystery of exactly how they pinpoint that boundless place thousands of kilometers away remains unsolved.

Another question remains: how do eels spawn? No one has ever directly observed them spawning in the Sargasso, nor has anyone captured it on camera. So how did scientists become so certain that this is their birthplace?

How Were Scientists So Sure Without Ever Seeing It?

The first clue to eel reproduction came from their larvae. Toward the end of the nineteenth century, in a laboratory in Italy, researchers watched for the first time as a leaf-like, transparent creature, a leptocephalus, slowly transformed into an eel in a tank.

It became clear that this ‘transparent leaf,’ once thought to be an entirely different animal or a sea worm, was in fact the eel’s larva. Now scientists had a way to trace the eel’s birthplace: wherever the smallest larvae are found, eels must be born.

The Danish scientist Johannes Schmidt followed exactly this lead. From 1904 to nearly 1924, he sailed ships across the Atlantic, cast nets in thousands of locations, and measured the larvae he caught, one by one.

After years of measurement, a clear pattern emerged: the farther from the Sargasso, the larger the larvae; the closer, the smaller. There was only one place where the smallest, newly hatched larvae were found: the middle of the Sargasso Sea.

In 1922, Schmidt published his conclusion that all Atlantic eels are born in the Sargasso. Many other lines of evidence now confirm this: DNA tests, chemical analysis of the larvae’s ear bones, and modern electronic tagging.

In 2022, scientists even managed to track tagged adult European eels to the vicinity of the Sargasso Sea.

Although eels have still not been observed spawning, the available evidence points to one conclusion: adult eels swim thousands of kilometers to reach the Sargasso. One night, at depths of roughly 400 to 1,000 meters, they release their eggs and sperm and then die.

Their bodies are rarely found. However, their young drift back toward the coasts on ocean currents. Once they mature, the same cycle begins again.

The Eel in Our Own Streams and the Mystery of the Indian Ocean

We have told the story of the eels of Europe and America, whose life cycle has been studied more than any other. But the eel’s saga, bound to the sea, is not limited to Europe and America. The eels in our own streams complete the same life cycle in a different sea.

There are about 16 species of eel worldwide, each tied to its own birthplace in the sea.

The eel found in South Asia is Anguilla bengalensis. Its journey is even longer. It descends from hill streams, joins great rivers like the Ganga and the Brahmaputra, crosses the plains, threads its way through the Sundarbans, the world’s largest delta, and passes through the Bay of Bengal into the deep Indian Ocean.

This journey, undertaken by an eel that looks so ordinary in our fields and streams, is one of the longest and least observed animal journeys in the world.

The Japanese eel (Anguilla japonica) makes a similar journey in the Pacific Ocean. Swimming two to three thousand kilometers from the rivers of East Asia, it reaches the West Mariana Ridge, an underwater mountain range, and spawns in the deep darkness around the new moon.

Now the biggest question arises: why do eels from Europe and America make such a long, grueling journey back to the same place, again and again?

This is where our eel becomes most intriguing. We know where European eels go: the Sargasso Sea. But science still does not know exactly which part of the Indian Ocean our eels reach to spawn. The Indian Ocean’s ‘Sargasso’ has yet to be found.

The Indian Ocean’s ‘Sargasso’ has yet to be found.

Atlantic eels spawn in a single area during a particular season. But our tropical eels appear to spawn year-round, possibly in different places.

That ordinary eel that suddenly appears in our fields during the monsoon rains carries within its body a mystery that the world’s great scientists have yet to solve.

Travelers in the Opposite Direction: Salmon and Hilsa

In scientific terminology, creatures that can live in both the salty water of the sea and the fresh water of rivers and streams are called ‘diadromous.’ Those, like the eel, that live in fresh water but migrate to the sea to spawn are called ‘catadromous.’

Fish with the exact opposite life cycle are called ‘anadromous.’ These fish live in the sea but migrate up rivers to spawn.

The best-known example of an anadromous fish is the salmon. It is born in freshwater, spends its adult life in the sea, and at spawning time returns to the very stream where it was born and dies there.

Interestingly, the eel uses the Earth’s magnetic field to find its way, while the salmon finds its way by the smell of the stream where it was born.

But you don’t have to go as far as the salmon to find a fish that travels in exactly the opposite direction of the eel. The famous hilsa, or ilish, of the Bay of Bengal makes just such a journey.

The eel travels down the Ganga and Brahmaputra toward the Bay of Bengal. By contrast, the hilsa moves up from that very bay along the same rivers, sometimes traveling more than 1,200 kilometers upstream to lay its eggs in freshwater.

In the same rivers and the same water, the eel and the hilsa travel in exactly opposite directions: one goes down to the sea to lay its young, the other climbs up the river to lay its own.

Though such a habit of crossing the border between salt and fresh water is rare, there are other examples. The Chinese mitten crab, like the eel, spends most of its life in rivers and migrates to the sea to breed.

Some turtles breed only after returning to the place where they were born. Fish such as the sea lamprey and the sturgeon, like salmon and hilsa, return to rivers to lay their eggs.

Crossing the border between salt and fresh water is not easy. To do so, the body must overhaul its entire salt-balancing system. That is why few creatures take such a risk. Those that do have, over millions of years of evolution, become specially adapted for this seemingly impossible journey.

Next monsoon, eels will return to our muddy fields. They are not ordinary fish wrapped in mud. Their bodies bear the imprint of an ancient sea, and their brains hold a magnetic map of the Earth.

Guided by a biological memory encoded in their DNA tens of millions of years ago, every eel will return thousands of kilometers to the same deep darkness of the ocean.

The eel’s true home was never the river. The truth about this creature that emerges from the mud was something Aristotle could not grasp and Freud could not find. Every eel carries within its body a journey and a mystery for which, even after thousands of years, today’s science still has no complete answer.

  • Lobsters Don’t Age: Telomerase, Telomeres and the Price of Living Forever
  • How a Salamander Regrows Its Limbs

title.$t: Faith Before Hunger

content.$t:
When Temples Gave Birth to Villages and Farming

Göbekli Tepe and Boncuklu Tarla suggest that belief and settled life came before the plough. We were taught that farming came first and temples came later. Ruins in Turkey suggest it may have been the other way around.

This awareness among women, that sowing seeds in the yard of one’s own hut and tending them was safer than roaming the forest, was in fact the starting point of agriculture.

This article was first published in Nepali on Ukaalo on February 5, 2026 (Magh 22, 2082 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: ukaalo.com ↗

What Turkey’s ancient sites suggest about how civilization began, at a glance.

We were always taught that the belly was filled first, and only then did people remember the gods. But 13,000-year-old ruins in Turkey have turned this story on its head. Discoveries at Göbekli Tepe and Boncuklu Tarla have shown that what bound people to one place was not the plow but faith. Some dismiss this as a ‘popular interpretation.’ This is a journey through 13,000-year-old drains, decorative jewelry, and even ‘piercings’ to a time when the ‘egg of faith’ was born before the ‘chicken’ of civilization.

Göbekli Tepe.

The Chicken, the Egg and Our Confusion

Which came first, the chicken or the egg? Many of us know this question well. But in seeking a simple answer, we usually get it wrong. Many find the answer easy: the chicken, because without a chicken an eggshell cannot form. Many of us know that the protein needed to build the outer part of the egg (such as ovocleidin-17) is found only in the body of a hen. On this basis, the usual conclusion is that an egg cannot be made without a chicken, so the chicken must have come first.

This is where our confusion lies: the conclusion is easy but incomplete. We treat the question as if it were about an event that happened suddenly at a single moment, but the evolution of living things is the result of a process of change that unfolds continuously over a long time.

Biology makes a different argument: the egg is far older than the chicken. Some 80–90 million years ago, in the age of the dinosaurs, and even earlier, as reptiles were evolving, these animals had already developed the ability to lay eggs. Only after thousands of generations of evolution among these reptiles did the chicken’s close ancestors appear.

The chicken is not an animal that appeared suddenly one day. It is simply the outcome of an evolutionary process, built from changes that accumulated gradually over many generations, and we have named it the chicken. In biological evolution, no species is separated from another by a clear line. The changes are small; humans give them names later.

The Evolution of Language and Biological Continuity

Comparing this with the history of language makes it even clearer. Latin did not suddenly become Italian one day. The first people did not learn Italian from their parents. They spoke a form of Latin that had been changing gradually. Latin shifted slowly: its sounds changed, its grammar was revised, its words took new forms, and one day we began calling that language ‘Italian.’ The parents of the first Italian speaker were not Italian, but today we call their children Italian. The name was new, but it was the continuation of an old process.

The chicken’s story is the same. The biological mechanism for producing eggshells already existed. A small genetic mutation occurred inside an egg, between two ‘almost-chickens.’ The mother’s body was already ‘almost-chicken,’ and the egg was already an ‘almost-chicken egg.’ The shell and the method were old, but the embryo inside crossed that small biological boundary, which, looking back later, we came to call ‘chicken.’ In this sense, the egg is not just a biological structure; it is a vessel of continuity, where the new is born within the old.

The egg is not just a biological structure; it is a vessel of continuity, where the new is born inside the old.

The Debate Over Civilization: Farming First, or Religion?

Which came first, the chicken or the egg? The same logic applies to the debate over civilization. At the beginning of human civilization, did farming come first, or faith and religion? As with the chicken and the egg, this question has long troubled anthropologists. We often treat names and institutions such as farming, religion, and cities as starting points. But civilization was not an invention that appeared suddenly in a single moment. Like the story of the chicken and the egg, civilization too began through a gradual process, slowly taking shape within old practices, beliefs, and ways of life.

Traditional maps of human history long placed the origin of civilization in the fertile region around Turkey’s Taurus Mountains and the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. The earliest human settlements were believed to have emerged in this region, known as the ‘Fertile Crescent,’ which curves like a half-moon across parts of today’s Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran. But recent excavations have pushed this story north of the Taurus Mountains, toward southern Anatolia in present-day Turkey.

Göbekli Tepe, Boncuklu Tarla and Karacadağ in southeastern Anatolia. The Fertile Crescent boundary is approximate.

About 13,000 years ago, people in the hills of southeastern Anatolia were not merely wandering hunters. They are now known as ‘complex foragers.’ They hunted, gathered wild grain, and moved with the seasons, yet returned again and again to the same area. It is in this very region, north of the Fertile Crescent, that we find the oldest evidence of farming, dating to about 13,000 years ago (11,000 BCE).

The Invention of Farming and the Role of Women’s Insight

About 12,000 years ago, the world was recovering from the Ice Age and beginning the ‘Holocene’ epoch. As the Ice Age ended, the Earth’s temperature began to rise, and as the ice melted, most of the land in the Northern Hemisphere became arable for the first time. Around this time, people who were caught between hunting and gathering, especially women, noticed something new: where wild seeds had fallen and been collected, new plants sprouted the following year again.

General historical knowledge tells us that farming did not begin all at once. This greatest change in human history did not start in a laboratory or through a sudden event. It resulted from thousands of years of careful observation and patience, and the credit goes mainly to women. While men traveled far to hunt, women gathered roots and wild grains around the settlement and began to observe the life cycle of plants up close. They were the first to understand that plants sprout and thrive best where fallen seeds mix with organic waste (manure).

This awareness among women that sowing seeds in the yard of one’s own hut and tending them was safer than roaming the forest was, in fact, the starting point of agriculture. Over thousands of years, women in hunter-gatherer groups selected the ‘good, non-shattering’ seeds of wild wheat, transforming it into domestic wheat and launching the age of farming. The discovery at the foot of Turkey’s Karacadağ mountains of DNA remains of the world’s oldest wheat, dating to nearly 13,000 years ago, also bears this out.

In this way, a small experiment that began with kitchen waste being thrown out eventually turned humans from ‘wanderers’ into ‘farmers.’ When people understood the relationship between seed and manure, humanity’s daring to take control of nature’s cycle began. Yet even the idea that civilization’s chicken hatched from this egg is incomplete.

Göbekli Tepe: When Faith Led the Plow

For a long time, historians believed one story: first people learned to farm, then they built permanent houses. Only when their granaries were full and they had leisure could they build temples and practice religion. In other words, ‘first the belly was filled, and only then were the gods remembered.’

But after the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began excavating at Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey in 1994, this account of our development was shaken to its roots. This roughly 12,000-year-old structure was not only the world’s first temple but also the first ‘3-D’ expression of human consciousness.

The giant T-shaped limestone pillars standing in circles, each weighing nearly ten tonnes, were not just shapeless stones; they were also faceless, human-like gods. The carved arms and meditative posture indicate that people of that time could already worship nature through symbols. Scorpions, foxes, and lions are carved on the pillars as if about to leap out of the stone, showing that people then did not merely fear nature but could understand and worship it in symbolic form.

Building the massive structures at Göbekli Tepe required hundreds, even thousands, of people. Who brought those hunters together, and why did they come? Göbekli Tepe unlocked one of history’s great mysteries: people first gathered in one place for religious or spiritual rituals, and that very gathering created the need for farming.

When Göbekli Tepe was built, people had not yet fully mastered farming. Excavations nearby have uncovered no permanent homes or farming tools. Yet thousands of people needed food while staying there for weeks to build the temple and hold festivals, and wild foods alone could not feed them. The need to feed these crowds may have led people to gradually domesticate the first grains, wheat and barley. Göbekli Tepe revealed a new possibility: the desire to build temples may have led people to become farmers.

For a long time, we believed that the chicken of human civilization hatched from the egg of ‘farming.’ But the discovery of Göbekli Tepe revealed a different egg: the egg of faith. What turned wanderers into settled communities was not the plow but a shared belief in an unseen power. Göbekli Tepe was the temple of hunters who carved gods in stone long before they learned to sow wheat.

The desire to build temples is what made people farmers.

Boncuklu Tarla: The First Foundation of Civic Life

Göbekli Tepe pushed history back 11,500 years. But Boncuklu Tarla, a human settlement discovered in 2008 in Turkey’s Mardin province, pushed the starting point of civilization even further back. The site is considered nearly 1,000 years older than Göbekli Tepe, or about 13,000 years old. While Göbekli was mainly a ritual center or temple, Boncuklu Tarla had already become a full-time ‘human settlement.’

Jewelry found at Boncuklu Tarla.

Evidence of permanent settlement missing at Göbekli Tepe has been found at Boncuklu Tarla. Its inhabitants had already begun building round houses, marking an early shift from ‘wandering’ to ‘settled’ life. They had also begun crafting early prototypes of the T-shaped pillars seen at Göbekli Tepe, showing that Göbekli Tepe’s grand structures were not built overnight but were the product of centuries of human labor.

Boncuklu Tarla has more than orderly housing. Most astonishing of all, researchers found an organized ‘drainage system’ there. That people built stone channels to keep their settlement clean some 13,000 years ago was no ordinary feat. It shows that those hill-dwelling hunter-gatherers had begun laying the groundwork for community health and permanent settlement long before they fully knew how to farm.

That people built stone channels to keep their settlement clean some 13,000 years ago was no ordinary thing.

The Origin of Identity and Ritual

We often think of early humans as mere creatures struggling to survive, but the people of Boncuklu Tarla were keenly aware of their ‘self’ and identity. Boncuklu Tarla literally means ‘field of beads.’ True to its name, more than a hundred thousand ornaments made of limestone, obsidian, and bone have been found at the site, which covers about thirty acres.

More interesting still, research published in 2024 shows that people there practiced ‘piercing,’ the ritual of piercing the body. When people began living in communities, they needed not only food and water but also identity and stability. Stone ornaments found near the ears and lower jaws of skeletons here provided the first evidence of body modification. These were not merely art: thousands of years before the first kings of Uruk wore crowns, people had already begun signaling their social status and individual identity.

Boncuklu Tarla proved that people of that time had not only an ‘ideal’ of worshipping gods but also developed a ‘principle’ of living together cleanly and in an orderly way. We did not settle in one place because we had plenty of food; rather, we gave up the wandering life in search of a new ‘ideal’ for human life. We wanted to be near those beads, to stay in the lap of our ancestors buried beneath the floors of our homes, and to live within the safety of an orderly environment.

The excavation of Boncuklu Tarla has revealed a new reality: building drains, stringing jewelry, and planning settlements were not pastimes taken up once the granaries were full. They were part of a search for a new ‘ideal’ of what human life should be, a search that began long before farming. If the search for an ‘ideal’ drew early humans to Göbekli Tepe, the egg of ‘principle’ had already formed at Boncuklu Tarla long before.

We did not settle in one place because we had plenty of food; we gave up the wandering life in search of a new ‘ideal’ of what human life should be.

Conclusion: The Continuous Transformation of Civilization

If we accept Göbekli Tepe as the ‘zero point’ of religion, Boncuklu Tarla can be considered the ‘zero point’ of civic life. The ‘zero point’ of human civilization was not a sudden explosion as we imagined. It is the result of a long, complex process in which our consciousness expanded, beginning at Boncuklu Tarla and branching out at Göbekli Tepe. Just as Italian needed hundreds of generations of ‘linguistic change’ to emerge from Latin, thousands of years of development, the beads of Boncuklu Tarla, the stone gods of Göbekli Tepe, and the grains of wheat that women preserved together prepared civilization’s common stage.

That is why agriculture, faith, and consciousness are bound together at the starting point of human civilization. In this sense, the ‘chicken’ (civilization) we have been looking for was not born from any single egg. It is the result of an endless bargain among many eggs: hunger and faith, personal identity and collective responsibility. The jewelry we wear today offers a glimpse of those 13,000-year-old ‘beads,’ and the engineering of modern cities bears the footprint of that first drain.

The real answer to the question asked at the start, ‘Which came first, the chicken or the egg?’, is perhaps this: ‘change’ comes first. The names (farming, religion, city) came later, but the human restlessness and dreams needed to create them already existed. This is how civilization’s chicken was born, in whose yard we stand today. We too remain a link in that same change, a journey that began in those hills of Anatolia and continues.

Read also

  • Between Two Rivers: How Mesopotamia Gave Birth to Civilization
  • Eridu, the First City of Sumer: From Flood to Fields
  • Kushim and Sukkalgir: The First Names Ever Written

title.$t: COVID-19, Long COVID and the Old Diseases It Reawakens

content.$t:
Your PCR test is negative, so why are you still exhausted? A new review suggests COVID may wake up viruses and TB that have been hiding in your body for years.

Once the virus has vanished from the body, or the PCR report has come back negative for COVID-19, why doesn’t the body signal that the war is over?

This article was first published in Nepali on Ukaalo on December 26, 2025 (Poush 11, 2082 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: ukaalo.com ↗

There have been studies on what the coronavirus (COVID-19) is and how it spreads, but much remains to be studied about the changes the body undergoes after a COVID-19 infection and about how long COVID develops. In this context, a paper published by Rutgers Medical College has raised a question and a suspicion: could the long-term effects seen after COVID-19 be caused not by COVID-19 alone, but by our own body’s hidden enemies that rise up during the infection?

COVID-19 and Its Link to SARS

Beginning in the Chinese city of Wuhan toward the end of 2019, the COVID-19 infection spread within a few months into a worldwide pandemic. First identified five years ago, COVID-19 has affected most of the world’s people directly or indirectly. COVID-19 was given the name ‘SARS-CoV-2.’ It is a respiratory virus, meaning it affects the respiratory system.

The virus that causes COVID-19 is called SARS-CoV-2 because of the SARS epidemic in China in 2002–03. COVID-19 and SARS are both respiratory diseases, and their effects are similar. SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, is structurally and genetically similar to SARS-CoV-1, the virus that causes SARS.

Unlike SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1 did not attach easily to human cells. Because researchers identified infections quickly, the epidemic did not spread worldwide. The SARS outbreak at that time was limited to about ten thousand infections, and nearly a thousand people died of it.

SARS-CoV-2 carries spike proteins on its outer surface that can easily attach to cells in our respiratory tract. Because of this ability, COVID-19 spreads more easily than SARS, and an infected person can quickly pass it on to others. That is why COVID-19 spread to every continent in such a short time.

Questions About COVID’s Long-Term Effects

In most people, a COVID infection lasts two to three weeks. Once COVID has healed, the body has cleared SARS-CoV-2. Even though our immune system has removed the virus, that doesn’t mean the infection’s effects are over. In some people, various problems continue for months afterward. These long-term effects of COVID-19 are what we call long COVID.

SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, cannot hide in our bodies. If the virus itself is no longer present, how do its long-term effects persist? Scientists are investigating this very question. In this context, a study recently published by researchers at Rutgers University has raised an important question: could long COVID be caused by COVID-19 reactivating other infections that were already hiding in the body?

The Structure of SARS-CoV-2 and How It Enters the Body

For most of us, COVID-19 begins when SARS-CoV-2 infects cells in the respiratory system. The virus can enter the body through the nose, mouth, or eyes via tiny droplets (aerosols) released when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks.

Once inside the body, the virus’s first target is the cells of the lungs and respiratory system, whose surfaces carry a protein called the ACE2 receptor. Normally, the ACE2 receptor helps cells with external signaling and biological regulation. But in COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2 uses this very ACE2 receptor as its main entry point into the cell.

SARS-CoV-2 is an RNA virus. Just as we keep our genetic information in the DNA of our chromosomes, some viruses store it in RNA. SARS-CoV-2 has no DNA and has no need for it. Its genome is positive-sense RNA at the virus’s core. Being positive sense means that once it enters a host cell, it can readily use the cell’s machinery to make viral proteins. At the start of infection, SARS-CoV-2 does not need to enter the host cell’s nucleus or make new DNA or extra RNA first.

The outside of SARS-CoV-2 is covered by a lipid viral envelope that protects the virus. Soap and water, alcohol, or hand sanitizer can kill the virus by disrupting this envelope. Inside the viral envelope, the membrane contains three types of protein: spike, membrane, and envelope proteins. Of these, the membrane and envelope proteins provide the virus’s structural protection. At the virus’s core is its RNA, wrapped and protected by the nucleocapsid protein.

The Spike Protein and the Start of Infection

Spike proteins are the most important part of SARS-CoV-2 infection. They are also why COVID-19 is called a coronavirus. They look like a crown (corona in Latin) on the virus’s outer surface and come in two types: spike-1 and spike-2. Spike-1 attaches to the host cell’s ACE2 receptor, while spike-2 helps fuse the virus and host cell membranes. Compared with SARS-CoV-1, the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the host cell’s ACE2 receptor much more easily and strongly. This is why COVID-19 spread across the world much more easily and quickly than SARS.

Once the virus’s spike protein binds to the host cell’s ACE2 receptor, a cell protease called TMPRSS2 becomes active. Able to cut proteins like scissors, it snips part of the spike protein, triggering the virus’s entry and opening the way for the viral RNA to enter the host cell.

In some cases, when TMPRSS2 is scarce, or the virus has mutated, the viral RNA can also enter the host cell through a process called endocytosis. The virus and the ACE2 receptor together form a small, spherical structure called an endosome, and the virus can enter the cell through this process. Omicron, which emerged after SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in Wuhan, mutated and infected cells through this same route.

How the Virus Copies Itself

Once the positive-sense RNA of SARS-CoV-2 reaches the host cell’s cytoplasm, it acts directly as messenger RNA and begins producing proteins. Using the host cell’s ribosomes, the viral RNA first produces the virus’s non-structural proteins. There are sixteen of them in total, and at the start of infection they are the virus’s main weapons. The non-structural proteins quickly begin to disrupt the host cell’s biological processes and redirect them toward viral replication. Early in infection, they build special structures inside the host cell that suppress the body’s early immune defenses and help speed up viral replication.

SARS-CoV-2 replicates differently from many other viruses. Its RNA is copied in the host cell’s cytoplasm. This virus never enters the cell’s nucleus and has no way to integrate into our DNA. As soon as SARS-CoV-2 infects a cell, the newly made proteins first build special structures inside it, whose membranes shield the viral RNA and its replication from the body’s immune system.

As soon as SARS-CoV-2 enters the cytoplasm of a human cell, it begins multiplying at extraordinary speed. Replication starts when an enzyme called RNA-dependent RNA polymerase makes a reverse (antisense) copy of the RNA. Using this as a template, forward (positive sense) copies of RNA, like those found in new viruses, are then made. Some of these RNAs are used again to make proteins, while others become the genomes of new viruses.

As COVID infection and viral replication progress, host cells become virtual virus factories. Their normal functions are gradually suppressed. The infected cells’ energy, amino acids, and ribosomes are all devoted to making new viruses. These cells eventually die, but not before producing large numbers of new viruses. The newly made viral particles leave the infected cells and spread the infection to nearby cells.

The Body’s Defense: War and Damage

A COVID-19 infection puts our body in a double bind. When infection begins, the body’s innate immune system (the early defense system) can recognize the virus’s proteins and RNA and produce cytokines, including interferons, to fight the virus. If the immune system recognizes the virus early and clears it quickly, a person has a chance of surviving a serious infection. The vaccines we receive are also intended for this purpose. But SARS-CoV-2 can suppress the body’s early defense system.

Once it begins infecting respiratory cells, the virus can produce many copies at once. COVID’s serious effects begin to appear when these newly made copies start attacking nearby cells. The infection becomes more complex, and the body’s adaptive immune system activates and joins the fight against the virus.

As the adaptive immune system begins fighting COVID in this way, serious effects start to appear in some people. In some, cytokine imbalance, blood vessel damage, and blood clotting set in, which can lead to acute respiratory syndrome, organ failure, and other serious effects. One way to understand it: becoming critically ill with COVID is the combined result of the COVID-19 virus and of the immune system fighting it.

Becoming critically ill with COVID is the combined result of the COVID-19 virus and of the immune system fighting it.

If our adaptive immune system does its job, COVID’s viral load gradually declines. After a COVID infection ends, remnants of SARS-CoV-2 do not persist in the body for long, and the virus cannot hide in the body’s cells or DNA. In almost everyone who has been infected and recovered, the virus’s RNA is gone from the body 14 to 21 days after infection.

This is the central question that puzzles science: once the virus has vanished from the body, or the PCR test comes back negative for COVID-19, why doesn’t the body signal that the war is over?

Long COVID: Why Do Problems Persist After Recovery?

SARS-CoV-2 has unique abilities that may cause many types of changes in the body. Problems that can appear later, even after COVID is over, because of changes that occurred during active infection are called long COVID, or in medical language, post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2.

The symptoms of long COVID are unusual and vary from person to person. Some feel extreme fatigue, while others experience brain fog: a clouded mind, loss of concentration, and difficulty thinking. After active SARS-CoV-2 infection ends, fragments of viral RNA have been found lingering in some cells outside the respiratory system (for example, in the gut, brain, or other tissues). These fragments can hide in small amounts for some time and continue to cause inflammation. Likewise, fragments of dead virus may remain in the body, and our immune system may keep attacking them as if they were live virus. This is also one reason people continue to sweat or feel persistent fatigue long after COVID is over.

Some people have also developed myocarditis, a serious inflammation of the heart muscle. Severe COVID infection also affects blood vessels. Microclots form in the vessels, blocking oxygen from reaching various organs. This is why some people have trouble breathing and feel fatigued for a long time. Damage to lung or heart tissue during the fight takes a long time to heal, and in some cases the immune system may go astray and attack the body’s own healthy cells (an autoimmune response).

The Rutgers Study: The Theory of ‘Immunity Theft’

There is another possibility. When the body’s entire defense system is focused on fighting the coronavirus, it loses its watch over other dormant viruses and bacteria that it has kept suppressed inside the body for years. As a result, just as prisoners escape when the jail guards leave, old infections, the criminals, get a chance to rise up again. The study suggests that long COVID may be caused not only by remnants of the coronavirus but also by hidden enemies reawakened by the body’s weakened immune state.

A detailed review by researchers at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School has examined this possibility: could this unbalanced immune state be the very foundation of long COVID? They conclude that some of long COVID’s serious symptoms are not caused by SARS-CoV-2 itself. In their review paper, they point out that these permanent but dormant viruses, bacteria, and other ‘dark antigens’ may have been reactivated because of immune disruption (immune hijacking) during the fight against COVID infection.

Remnants of Old Diseases Hidden in Our DNA

If we turn the pages of our human genetic makeup (DNA) and read it as the biography of our chromosomes, we find that its earliest chapters were written by viruses. It may sound surprising, but a large part of our DNA is, in fact, a ‘viral remnant.’ Much of our DNA consists of the remains of ancient infections: fragments of prehistoric retroviruses, broken viral enzymes, and scattered genetic husks. Our DNA is not a clean page; it is a ‘historical manuscript’ in which viruses have written their stories. So it would be no exaggeration to say we are half human and a little bit ‘virus.’

Some viruses and bacteria have evolved the ability to hide within DNA itself. For example, retroviruses such as HIV, which can cause AIDS, can integrate their DNA into our chromosomes, where it can remain for life and be passed on to future generations. The remnants of ancient retroviruses that infected our bodies have made a permanent home in our DNA as transposons, or jumping genes.

Our DNA is not a clean page; it is a ‘historical manuscript’ in which viruses have written their stories.

Some bacteria or viruses can enter the cell’s nucleus and use its DNA-copying machinery but cannot integrate into the DNA. Some viruses associated with respiratory diseases have this ability. Some viruses (EBV, CMV) and some bacteria (TB), though unable to do either, suppress their own protein production to evade the immune system’s surveillance and have developed the ability to hide in various cells and persist in our bodies for life.

As I said at the start of this article, the virus that causes COVID-19 has no such ability, but its infection can trigger many changes in the body. First, even before serious infection sets in, the virus can remodel chromatin in the body’s immune cells. Put simply, the virus can change how the cell’s instruction manual is read or used. Such immune remodeling may leave long-term effects on the immune system. In a sense, COVID-19 is not only a respiratory disease but also an immune disease.

Chromatin remodeling can disrupt cytokine balance, creating long-term obstacles to the development of monocytes that recognize viruses and to the development of T and B cells that fight them. Even after the remnants of SARS-CoV-2 are gone from the body, transcriptional processes (how DNA becomes RNA and protein) that were altered during the infection remain distorted. Think of it this way: the immune system has already learned the wrong lesson and cannot unlearn it.

Immunity Theft: War at the Border, Insecurity in the City

Another long-term effect of COVID-19 is the very immune system that clears the infection. During a complex, acute COVID-19 infection, a biological state of emergency takes hold inside our bodies. As soon as SARS-CoV-2 attacks, the body’s entire defense machinery, especially T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells, drops other work and concentrates on the front lines in the lungs and respiratory system. After a COVID-19 infection, the body’s immune system is weakened: its soldiers have either been killed in battle or are utterly exhausted.

This is where the body’s security system slips up badly in the fight against SARS-CoV-2. In scientific terms, this is called immune distraction. Imagine the country’s entire army is busy at the border fighting a foreign enemy (the coronavirus). At such a time, internal security in the capital and other cities weakens, and hidden enemies within get a chance to rise up. The same happens in our bodies. This study has raised the question and the suspicion that the danger of long-term effects after COVID may come not from an outside enemy but from remnants of old viruses that have slept in our own bodies for thousands of years, waking up again.

The danger may come not from an outside enemy but from remnants of old viruses that have slept in our own bodies.

When the body’s immune system unites to fight COVID-19, the process by which it keeps constant watch over the body (immune surveillance) weakens. The Rutgers study calls this ‘immunity theft’ by COVID. The period of COVID infection thus becomes a major hole in the immune system, the security apparatus that keeps constant watch over the body. Hidden enemies take advantage of this very hole, which can give rise to latent tuberculosis, retroviruses, herpes viruses, or the Epstein-Barr virus. Lymphopenia, the shortage of white blood cells seen in COVID patients, widens this security vacuum even further.

About 8 percent of our DNA consists of remnants of ancient retroviruses that infected our ancestors millions of years ago and later became part of our genome. Normally, our body keeps them silent by placing an epigenetic lock on them.

But the immunity theft caused by COVID-19 can break those locks. As a result, these ancient viruses or transposons become active and start producing their own proteins. In this state, the body’s immune system treats even proteins made from its own DNA as foreign and begins to attack them. The study points to a strong possibility that some of the autoimmune problems seen in long COVID, in which the body attacks its own healthy organs, may be caused by these hidden enemies reawakening.

Hidden Enemies: Tuberculosis and Other Viruses

Retroviruses can integrate into our DNA and be passed down through the generations, but many other hidden enemies can also lie dormant in the body, waiting for a chance to become active again. Among these, the reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) has made the symptoms of long COVID even more mysterious.

About 95 percent of adults worldwide have been infected with EBV. Likewise, CMV has infected 85 percent of the world’s people. Our immune system recognizes this childhood infection and clears it easily. Even so, small amounts of the virus may persist and remain hidden in the body for life. Normally, in almost everyone infected, our immune system’s surveillance keeps these small amounts of lingering virus in check.

When the body’s immune system digs in to fight COVID-19, immune surveillance weakens elsewhere in the body, and these old, opportunistic viruses lying dormant get a chance to rise up. As the Rutgers study shows, when COVID-19 erodes the function of the immune system’s soldiers—the T, B, and natural killer cells—EBV can be reawakened. This may be why the rate of patients arriving at hospitals with reactivated EBV has been rising by ten percent every year since the COVID pandemic.

The brain fog, extreme fatigue, and neurological weakness that long COVID patients experience closely resemble the symptoms of active EBV. Likewise, when CMV becomes active, it causes inflammation in blood vessels and accelerates the entire immune system’s aging (immune aging). This is why, even at 30 or 40, the body can begin to feel the fatigue and weakness of someone aged 60 or 70.

For a country like Nepal, however, the most worrying issue is the reactivation of latent tuberculosis, or latent TB. In a large part of our population, TB bacteria lie dormant within small nodules (granulomas) in the lungs. The excessive inflammation that COVID-19 brings risks breaking down the structure of these nodules that keep the bacteria confined. Just as prisoners escape when the jail walls crumble, these bacteria begin to spread through the lungs.

This is where the problem becomes even more complicated. The symptoms of active TB and long COVID (a persistent cough, evening fevers, weight loss, and extreme fatigue) are very similar. As a result, patients and doctors may mistake them for the ordinary after-effects of COVID, or simply long COVID. This study makes us seriously consider that if health problems persist for a long time after COVID, they may not be just the virus’s effect but tuberculosis that COVID has awakened. Therefore, when managing long COVID patients in Nepal, TB testing should be a mandatory priority.

For a country like Nepal, the most worrying issue is the reactivation of latent tuberculosis.

Another Danger: Immune Amnesia After COVID

Another far-reaching and frightening effect of COVID-19 infection is immune amnesia, or immune forgetting. Just as old files are lost when a computer is formatted, a severe COVID-19 infection can damage our immune system’s memory bank.

As mentioned in the Rutgers review, there are signs that COVID, like measles, can wipe out the body’s store of memory B cells and antibodies. This means that after COVID-19, our bodies may forget the vaccines we received in childhood or the diseases we fought and beat in the past. As a result, even after recovering from COVID, people remain at risk of easily falling prey to pneumonia, the flu, or other common infections.

In the end, we must understand that COVID-19 turns out to be more than just a viral infection. A COVID-19 infection can also trigger an imbalance in the body’s immune system and awaken enemies that have hidden in our genes and bodies since ancient times. In treating long COVID, which appears sometime after COVID, there now seems to be a need for diagnosis and treatment that accounts not only for the coronavirus but also for the old infections it has reawakened. COVID-19 has taught us a new lesson: the virus may be gone, but we still have much to prepare before we can fight the biological shadow it leaves behind.

(This article focuses on the question raised by this research published from Rutgers.)

Read also

  • The Viruses That Settle in Our Bodies, Part 2
  • Why Does the Body Treat a New Kidney as an Enemy?
  • Dark antigens and Transposons
