title.$t: Cousin Marriage & Genetic Disease

content.$t:
From Tutankhamun to the Habsburgs, How endogamy shrinks our Genetic Pool

We humans have come this far by surviving many kinds of catastrophe over our evolution. Having split from the common ancestor we share with the other primates, the apes, nearly 5 million years ago, we are very new…

*Japan’s imperial family once had a custom of marrying only within four particular families. Lasting nearly eight hundred years, the practice left imperial family members shorter on average than other Japanese.*

This article was first published in Nepali on Ukaalo on December 4, 2025 (Mangsir 18, 2082 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: ukaalo.com ↗

How marrying within the family brings hidden recessive genes together, from Tutankhamun’s dynasty to the Habsburg jaw and Queen Victoria’s hemophilia.

We humans have come this far by surviving many kinds of catastrophe over our evolution. Having split from the common ancestor we share with the other primates, the apes, nearly 5 million years ago, we are very new compared with many other species in nature. We became modern humans by enduring the genetic bottleneck caused by the Toba volcano and climate change, the harshness of the Ice Age, and countless geographic hardships and barriers. Our species, Homo sapiens, emerged only about 300,000 years ago.

Genetic Diversity Narrowed by Endogamy

We made it this far by weathering harsh external conditions, but humankind has also built countless walls within itself, further narrowing our genetic diversity. In my previous article, I explained why human genetic diversity is lower than that of other animals. The practice of protecting the purity of one’s lineage and community, carried on in various guises since the dawn of civilization, has also increased the risk of a range of hereditary diseases.

Our ancestors spent much of the primitive age as hunters. For a long time, our evolution proceeded without these boundaries. Only after a woman from a hunting group living around Turkey’s Taurus Mountains first learned to farm, nearly fifteen thousand years ago, did ‘civilization’ begin. As civilization expanded, the desire to maintain ‘ties’ with one’s clan, religion, caste, community, or royal line became part of our nature.

We began marrying within our own clan, caste, community, and religion (endogamy). The genetic diversity that nature’s randomness increases was steadily narrowed by such boundaries as society developed. But a tradition begun to protect the identity and purity of a community or lineage has, over time, become a genetic prison. Here is the paradox of our evolution: the farther we spread geographically, the more we narrowed our genetic diversity through geographic, social, and cultural structures of every kind. This harmed the development of humankind.

As kingship took hold in ancient civilizations, the tradition of marrying within one’s own family to preserve the purity of the royal line also began. This practice of marrying within one’s own family or among close relatives-first among kings and later among ordinary people as well-further reduced our already limited genetic diversity, and several genetic diseases appeared as a result.

A tradition begun to protect the identity and purity of a community or lineage has, over time, turned into a genetic prison.

Tutankhamun’s Tomb and the Evidence

Many people interested in ancient Egypt will have heard the name ‘Tutankhamun.’ Tut was briefly king (pharaoh) of Egypt. After his death, the tomb containing his mummy (a body preserved so it would not decay for a long time) lay sealed in the desert for nearly four thousand years. Archaeologists found it ‘just as it was’ in 1922. It was the first pharaoh’s tomb untouched by robbers, which is one reason his name is so well known. Behind his fame, above that of Egypt’s other kings and pharaohs, lies a remarkable natural coincidence.

Those who study ancient Egypt divide its nearly three thousand years of civilization into three main periods-the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms. Say ‘Egypt,’ and we think of its pyramids. But pharaohs were buried in pyramids only during the first few centuries of Egypt’s Old Kingdom. From the Middle Kingdom onward, pyramid robbers became a plague. From then on, the custom was to lay dead kings to rest in the ‘Valley of the Kings,’ far from the pyramids on the Giza plateau. Tut, who died at just 18 or 19, was a pharaoh of ancient Egypt’s last era, the New Kingdom.

Behind his name being better known than those of all of Egypt’s other kings and pharaohs lies a remarkable natural coincidence.

Most pharaohs’ tombs did not escape the tomb robbers who came later. By the time excavators found and opened them, robbers had usually already carried off the mummies and other offerings. Tut’s body, too, had been laid in the ‘Valley of the Kings.’ A few years after Tut died, a huge flood came down the Nile and submerged the Valley of the Kings for the first time. Because of that flood, no one could open Tut’s tomb, sealed for four thousand years, until the beginning of the twentieth century.

Inside the tomb were not only his mummy but also many other offerings, all well preserved. Studying Tut’s body and the other objects found in the tomb provided, for the first time, solid evidence that during Egypt’s New Kingdom the royal family married within the family (inbreeding) to preserve the purity of its ‘divine lineage.’ Examining Tut’s body revealed that his parents were full brother and sister. Tut, who died young, had been born with weak feet; his bones were abnormal, and he had other physical weaknesses as well.

Tut is evidence that the rulers of Egypt’s New Kingdom married within their own family for a long time. This practice, carried on for generations to preserve the ‘divine purity’ of the royal line, has been found to have left many physical disorders in the bodies of other pharaohs as well. Tut, it turns out, died young because of genetic disorders caused by long-running inbreeding. His tomb also held the mummies of his sister-wife and of two daughters who died in the womb. All three had congenital disorders like Tut’s, and many others besides.

The ancient Egyptian tradition of preserving the ‘divine lineage’ also reached later royal courts. Nearly four thousand years ago, Egypt’s pharaohs knew nothing of genetics. Like Tut, many other New Kingdom pharaohs also died young because of genetic diseases. Genetic diseases also played an important role in the fall of ancient Egypt. The Greek (Ptolemaic) rulers who came to govern Egypt after Alexander conquered it continued this pharaonic tradition. Cleopatra is the Ptolemaic dynasty’s famous queen. The Roman emperor Julius Caesar made both Egypt and Cleopatra his own. Before marrying Cleopatra, Caesar defeated her own brother-husband in war.

For some royal families, the purity of the lineage mattered more than anything else, and this practice and belief endured for a very long time. The custom of Egypt’s royal house continued into Greek and Roman civilization as well. Much later, it appears widely among Europe’s royal families too.

The Habsburg family, which once ruled Spain, long maintained the practice of marrying within the family to preserve the royal family’s ‘divine purity.’ The effects of their inbreeding appeared in all their descendants-a deformed jaw, also known as the ‘Habsburg jaw.’ Their rule perished with Charles III, who died of a genetic disease caused by inbreeding.

It was not only in Europe. Japan’s imperial family, too, once had a custom of marrying only within four families of the capital. Only after the Second World War did they realize that this practice, which lasted nearly eight hundred years, had left members of the imperial family, on average, shorter than other Japanese. Only then did they begin encouraging imperial family members to marry outside those families wherever possible.

The custom begun to protect the ‘purity’ of royal lineages was not confined to palaces. Community norms we still see-that one may marry only within the same religion, caste or community, or only if the combination of gotra, varna and nakshatra matches-are its remnants. Endogamy, the practice of marrying only within one’s own caste, religion or community, gradually took deep root in society. Unscientific traditions like this, begun to protect social identity and family purity, played the most important role in eroding people’s ability to fight disease.

Marriage Among Relatives and the Risk of Hereditary Disease

The secret of the genetic diseases passed down the generations lies hidden in our DNA. Almost all of us have the same twenty-three pairs of chromosomes. Within these chromosomes, DNA contains nearly 35 million nucleotides and nearly thirty thousand protein-coding genes. Which genes work, and the proteins they make, determine every kind of cell in the body, the types of organs, and the body’s many processes. Not every gene works all the time, though; in any cell of the body, only about ten thousand genes are at work at any one moment.

Each gene comes in two copies, called alleles: one from the mother and the other from the father. Which allele gets to work, and when, plays an important role in what the gene does. The two alleles rarely work at the same time, and they cannot both work with equal strength. This property is why alleles come in two types-effective (dominant) and ineffective (recessive). Most of the time, dominant alleles keep the recessive alleles of genes that could harm the body in check.

Most hereditary diseases-like Tut’s deformed body and those of Europe’s Habsburgs-appear when these recessive alleles become active. How these harmful recessive alleles come into play depends on how they are passed down through generations.

Children born to parents from unrelated families have a low chance of inheriting such a recessive disease. The custom of marrying the children of one’s paternal and maternal uncles (consanguineous marriage) still exists in some Muslim-majority countries and in some of our own communities. Marriage between close relatives, or marriage limited to a particular community, causes recessive alleles to surface and increases the likelihood of other diseases. If the children of one’s maternal uncle, paternal aunt, paternal uncle, or maternal aunt marry, the chance of recessive genes surfacing in their children rises by about twenty percent.

Hemophilia in Europe’s Royal Courts

One example of a disease that appears because of marriage among close relatives is the ‘royal disease,’ hemophilia. First appearing in Britain’s Queen Victoria, this disease spread to all of Europe’s royal families after her. Hemophilia is caused by mutations in genes on the X chromosome that produce the proteins needed for blood clotting. Because this recessive mutation affects only one allele on the X chromosome, it does not show in women, who have two X chromosomes. Queen Victoria carried this allele, but its effect did not show in her.

In Victoria, the recessive allele carrying the hemophilia mutation was kept in check by the dominant, non-mutated allele of the same gene. The recessive mutation she carried was passed down to her descendants. Each of her sons had a 50 percent chance of having hemophilia, and each of her daughters had a 50 percent chance of being a carrier like Victoria. Hemophilia took Victoria’s son Leopold young. Her daughters married princes across Europe, which is how this royal disease reached so many of Europe’s royal courts. Many other genetic diseases-cystic fibrosis, thalassemia, and others-are passed down the generations in the same way as hemophilia.

High Disease Rates in Communities That Practice Cousin Marriage

In children born to first-cousin marriages, harmful recessive alleles and the mutations they carry surface in exactly this way, and it is their effect that causes most hereditary and genetic diseases. X and Y chromosomes are passed down a little differently from the others, but in short, for these recessive diseases to appear, both parents must carry the disease-causing alleles. Marrying a close relative further increases the chance that both carry those alleles. In consanguineous marriages, the chance of genetic disease rises by 1.7 to 2.8 times.

For these recessive diseases to appear, both parents must carry the disease-causing alleles.

This custom still exists in some countries where Islam is practiced, and many of these countries show high rates of diabetes. Diabetes comes in two types, and their causes differ. One type, type 2 diabetes, is caused by defects in the genes that make insulin. The traditional custom of consanguineous marriage raises the chance that defects in the genes needed to make insulin are present in both alleles. In communities that practice consanguineous marriage, many of these recessive alleles carry mutations in pairs, and the resulting defects can cause insulin resistance and disrupt the balance of glucose metabolism, leading to type 2 diabetes.

The Lesson of History

Practices like these, carried out in various guises to preserve the purity of communities and lineages, gradually eroded the human species’ ability to fight many diseases. This custom of endogamy, which continues even today, shrank communities’ effective population size, narrowed our gene pool, and allowed harmful hereditary mutations to accumulate.

Some communities, however, have social rules that discourage marriage between close relatives. The Hindu-Sanatani rule in Nepal against marrying within the same gotra is one example. (Even so, while keeping apart by surname and gotra is the right thing to do, marrying only within the same caste or community is still tied to ‘blood purity.’) Sharing a gotra means having common ancestors who later split into different surnames. In most north Indian communities-Brahmin, Kayastha, Baniya, Vaishya, Rajput, and others-marriage within the same gotra is also ‘forbidden,’ although further south, marriage within the same gotra is accepted in some places. But we must also understand this: you might fool God by having a pandit recite mantras, but DNA does not recognize those mantras.

You might fool God by having a pandit recite mantras, but DNA doesn’t recognize them.

Pakistan’s high rate of type 2 diabetes is also due to consanguineous marriage. In our own country, too, the communities practice marrying the children of a maternal uncle, paternal aunt, paternal uncle, or maternal aunt. In those communities, high rates of diabetes, like those seen in Pakistan, along with other genetic diseases, have also been observed. The custom still exists in some Muslim countries. As genetic knowledge grows, the practice is declining. Thanks to education and awareness, DNA testing before marriage-even when a consanguineous marriage cannot be avoided-has also become more common to prevent genetic diseases that can arise when recessive alleles are expressed.

Mismatches in the balance between dominant and recessive genes do not occur only among relatives; anyone can face the risk of such genetic diseases when their recessive alleles happen to match. Anyone who wants to have a child can now get tested to find out whether the child could have genetic diseases. What’s more, where future children are found to be at risk of such diseases, new methods, including CRISPR, have emerged that can remove those mutations from the allele.

In the name of tradition-whether for a throne, a caste, or a clan-the genetic diversity we have lost is the very foundation of our existence. Today we stand at a crossroads where ancient tradition meets modern science. Whether by widening our social circle to embrace those beyond our narrow community or by using modern genetic screening (DNA testing), we have the power to tear down these self-made walls. We must not blindly repeat the mistakes of the pharaohs or the Habsburgs; the walls of this genetic prison must come down.

Read also

  • How DNA Copies Itself
  • Rosalind Franklin

title.$t: Why Does the Body Treat a New Kidney as an Enemy?

content.$t:
Your immune system can’t tell a life-saving kidney from an invader. Here’s why transplant patients take immune suppressants for life, and why one rare side effect doesn’t justify a sweeping claim

All medicines and their side effects cannot be lumped together and discussed in one breath. And for a physician who has worked in this very field for a long time to make an absurd pronouncement is even more shameful.

This article was first published in Nepali on Ukaalo on November 13, 2025 (Kartik 27, 2082 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: ukaalo.com ↗

Your immune system can’t tell a life-saving kidney from an invader. Here’s why transplant patients take immune suppressants for life, and why one rare side effect doesn’t justify a sweeping claim.

After a kidney or any other organ transplant, a person must take immunosuppressants (drugs that suppress the immune system) for life. Immunosuppressants can also cause side effects, and extensive research has been done on them. As someone who understands how the immune system and immunosuppressants work, I have written about them here to clear up a public misconception about a side effect of immunosuppressants that occurs in fewer than 5 percent of people.

Why Does the Body Need Its Kidneys?

When it comes to removing almost every kind of waste that enters the body, the kidney is the most important organ. We all have two kidneys; in women, each kidney weighs about 135 grams, while in men, they are slightly larger, about 150 grams.

The kidney’s job is not just to remove the body’s waste. It also plays an important role in regulating blood pressure, electrolyte balance, and hormonal balance, and in bone development. It is ideal if both kidneys perform the same work; otherwise, a single kidney can do the job too.

The kidney’s capacity to clear waste is also limited; if it has to filter more than it can handle in a day, it comes under extra strain. Many people mistakenly believe that drinking lots of water is good for the body and the kidneys. It is true that drinking too little water is bad for both the kidneys and the body. Drink water as needed, but drinking a lot of it does not make the kidneys any better.

Physical imbalances in our bodies, for various reasons, gradually erode the kidneys’ ability to filter waste. In all of us, kidney function declines not only because of kidney disease but also because of age, diet, and nutritional imbalance. In the context of this article, the state in which both kidneys can no longer work is understood as ‘kidney failure.’

Once the kidneys that filter the body’s waste stop working, one cannot survive for long. In some cases, dialysis can extend kidney function for days or months and prolong life, but that too is not a permanent solution.

Transplant, Transplant Rejection and Immune Suppressants

The permanent solution for kidney failure is a new kidney- that is, a ‘kidney transplant.’ When both of someone’s kidneys stop working, ‘borrowing’ a kidney from someone else and putting it in is a kidney transplant. If the first transplanted kidney does not work, those who can afford it sometimes get yet another new kidney. We have all heard about the ordeal of where and how a kidney is ‘borrowed’; let’s not go there today.

A new kidney has to be transplanted- but where would it come from? None of us has more than two kidneys! Yet our bodies can function well with just one healthy kidney. Someone with two healthy kidneys donates one to a patient whose kidneys have failed. But as soon as a new kidney is transplanted, the body does not recognize it right away.

All of us have an inborn defense system (immune system) in our bodies. It is this immune system that recognizes a new kidney as a foreign substance (foreign object) and tries to reject it. Why the immune system attacks a new kidney as a foreign substance- or why a kidney donated by as close a relative as possible is said to be best- I will reveal in the last section of this article.

Because of this attack by the immune system, a kidney transplant can fail. Since the new kidney comes from another person, there is always a chance the immune system will reject it. That is why patients who have had an organ transplant must take medicine to prevent this (immune suppressants) for life. These drugs are used mainly to reduce the activity of T cells—the core soldiers of the immune system- and have a wide variety of effects. Because each drug has different effects, there are naturally many co-effects and side effects too.

Our country’s former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, underwent a second kidney transplant some years ago, possibly in India. I had heard somewhere an ‘indigestible comment’ made by a senior doctor who has long worked on kidneys, about a side effect of the immunosuppressants Oli had to take after his transplant.

Surely that doctor sahib must have studied the difference between a drug’s effect and its side effect! It is well known that many people spread medical and health rumors on social media due to a lack of knowledge, but what I could not accept was the jab from a doctor like him, linking a side effect of immune suppression to someone’s mental health.

He surely knows more than I do about kidney failure. But I also know at least a little about organ transplants, transplant rejection, and immunosuppressants. As a researcher in this field, I have made an effort to write what I know.

A Side Effect of Immune Suppressants: Reactivation of EBV and Other Viruses

There is a virus called the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) that is associated with cancer. This is what I work on. This virus infects everyone in childhood.

The immune system detects an EBV infection in early childhood quickly and easily. It recognizes EBV as a foreign antigen and launches an attack to destroy the virus. In this way, our immune system clears EBV and reduces the viral load in one go. This process is called immune clearance. Because our immune system clears EBV so easily in childhood, an early EBV infection usually goes unnoticed.

Immune clearance, however, is rarely one hundred percent. Some EBV can hide dormant inside the blood’s B cells (immune escape). They remain inactive, shutting down their programs for making viral proteins. We all carry EBV- some in small amounts, some in somewhat larger amounts.

In everyone, childhood EBV infection also leaves an imprint on the immune system. After EBV first infects us, immune cells that recognize it are formed, and their constant vigilance keeps the hidden virus from reactivating.

All of us always carry EBV- some in small amounts, some in somewhat larger amounts.

Everyone who has had an organ transplant takes drugs that weaken the immune system- immune suppressants. But when do you ever get a laddu in both hands? On the one hand, without immune suppressants, organ rejection puts the patient’s very life at risk. On the other hand, taking immune suppressants to avoid that raises the chance that EBV and many other viruses lying dormant in the transplant recipient’s DNA will become active again.

EBV is a cancer-causing virus. Reactivated EBV can cause cancer in the B cells of the blood. When EBV reactivates, it drives uncontrolled B-cell growth, which is called EBV lymphoma. It is like the tumor of other cancers; if it keeps growing, it can take the form of cancer. Although such cancer doesn’t occur under normal conditions, transplant patients on immunosuppressants face a higher chance of this cancer- PTLD (post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease). The chance of PTLD with immunosuppressants after a kidney transplant is now considered to be less than about one percent.

One side effect of immunosuppressants is EBV reactivation and PTLD. At first glance, then, using immunosuppressants carries a risk that EBV becomes active and causes PTLD. And PTLD is a type of cancer.

Is it fair to flatly declare that immunosuppressants cause cancer? It is not that PTLD never occurs with immunosuppressants, but it doesn’t occur in everyone. Before declaring that they cause cancer, it is important to understand that the likelihood is less than 1 percent- and, knowing this, not to mislead anyone.

Tacrolimus, an Immunosuppressive Drug: The Difference Between Its Effects and Side Effects

Every medicine is made for a specific purpose, and its aim is usually a good one. Beyond a drug’s intended effect, almost every drug carries the possibility of co-effects and side effects. Some drugs have few side effects, while others have many. Side effects can also differ depending on the type and brand of the drug. A drug designed to weaken the very immune system that protects our body is bound to have certain side effects.

Before declaring that they cause cancer, it is important to understand that the likelihood is less than 1 percent- and, knowing this, not to mislead anyone.

In transplants, tacrolimus is most commonly used as the immunosuppressant. It works by inhibiting calcineurin, a protein important for T cells, the immune system’s soldiers. Its use also causes other side effects. Besides PTLD, with its less-than-1-percent chance discussed earlier, the likelihood of other side effects is about the same.

Tacrolimus is not a new drug; the FDA, the agency that approves drugs in the United States, cleared it for use in 1994. Many studies have examined the side effects that can come with its use, and these must continue to be reported. Doctors who prescribe tacrolimus are aware of these side effects. That is why everyone who has had a transplant also takes additional medicines alongside the immunosuppressant to prevent side effects.

It should also be understood that a medicine taken for life does not have to be taken at the same dose forever. In the first few years after a transplant, the risk of organ rejection is somewhat higher. As the body gradually gets used to the new organ, that risk keeps falling. At that stage, doctors also gradually reduce the tacrolimus dose.

I don’t know exactly which medications former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli takes after his kidney transplant. I can only guess that he likely uses tacrolimus in combination with drugs to protect against its known side effects.

As the doctor mentioned above said, tacrolimus does have side effects. But the likelihood is small- less than 5 percent. In other words, out of a hundred people taking tacrolimus, five might develop the kind of illness he spoke of.

In such a situation, my ethics would certainly not allow me to call a tacrolimus user a patient with PTLD cancer, whose likelihood is less than 15. To me, it is not justified for the doctor sahib either to pick out a side effect with less than a 5 percent chance and pronounce on someone’s mental balance. The doctor himself should know a drug’s effects and side effects, its dosage, and that one must not tell someone ‘You have this illness’ without even making a diagnosis.

Let us understand a little more about why tacrolimus or similar drugs must be used when transplanting a kidney or another organ.

How Does Our Immune System Work?

As I said at the beginning of the article, our innate defense system recognizes and distinguishes the body’s ‘own’ (self) substances from ‘foreign’ ones. Our immune system, including the white blood cells (WBCs) in our blood, is highly agile, but for it to work, many types of immune cells must come together in the right balance.

The immune system includes many kinds of immune cells, including T cells among the WBCs, all working together. They keep constant watch and carry information to the T cells that fight threats. For the body’s defense system to work, the many roles of each immune cell, their effects, and the interplay between those effects must come together.

Our first shield (defense system) is our innate immune system (innate immunity). From the day we are born, it protects us from all kinds of foreign substances (viruses, bacteria, allergens, and so on). Macrophages and neutrophils, which we count in a blood test or blood report, and complement proteins, also found in tears and sweat, are part of innate immunity. Although innate immunity is always active and can fight many threats, it doesn’t recognize specific invaders and is not very effective.

The adaptive immune system (adaptive immunity) is our second layer of protection, and it is far more powerful than innate immunity. Adaptive immunity begins its work only after its first contact with a foreign substance. Once it has come into contact with a foreign substance, however, adaptive immunity recognizes it specifically and stores its memory forever.

Antigen-Presenting Cells and HLA

To recognize foreign substances (antigens), a class of cells- monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, and others- should be understood as antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Constantly circulating on patrol, these cells recognize foreign antigens and carry them to the cells that can confront the external threat. The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on APCs plays an important role in recognizing foreign antigens.

In humans, MHC is called the human leukocyte antigen (HLA). They are perhaps the most important players in adaptive immunity. They remember every vaccine we have received and every disease we have had. Not only that- the memory of diseases that struck our ancestors long ago and the ability to survive them are also embedded in them.

Because we evolved from small, limited early ancestors, we don’t have much HLA diversity. Even so, HLA genes are the most polymorphic of all- many times more so than any other genes. Their polymorphism comes from the many combinations of countless alleles of HLA’s three main genes. To a large extent, the greater the HLA diversity, the stronger our immunity tends to be.

Greater HLA diversity generally leads to stronger immunity.

HLA also comes in two types, HLA-I and HLA-II. HLA-I presents antigens only to CD8 T cells, while HLA-II presents them only to CD4 T cells. On the surface of both types of T cells is another important molecule, the TCR, which must recognize both the HLA and the foreign antigen it presents. Because HLA must recognize the foreign antigen before the TCR does, HLA diversity is also the main driver of TCR diversity.

B Cells and T Cells: The Soldiers of Adaptive Immunity

The first soldiers of adaptive immunity to fight external attacks are B cells. By making antibodies, they target pathogens, including bacteria and viruses. They also have a kind of memory, through antibodies, for fighting a threat they have recognized before. The antibodies that B cells make from new and old encounters with external pathogens help activate CD4 and CD8 cells. But when B cells become active and make antibodies, the bigger effect is activating natural killer cells.

The most effective roles in adaptive immunity are played by the two types of CD3-bearing cells- CD8 and CD4 T cells. Of the two, CD8 T cells are somewhat more active, and CD4 T cells are generally thought to play only a supporting role for CD8 T cells in most situations.

CD4 T cells come in many types and perform many functions. In the context of cancer, depending on their location in the body and the type of cancer, some may play a helpful role while others may be unhelpful. These days, it is increasingly accepted that CD4 cells are not just helpers but can also attack cancer cells directly. There is a type of CD4 cell that can continue working to a large extent even under heavy immune suppression. These are called cytotoxic CD4 cells.

My research aims to determine whether these cells can be used to treat cancers such as PTLD. The reason my research uses CD4 rather than the more effective CD8 is that immunosuppressants and immunocompromising factors like HIV affect CD4 cells more severely. Another reason is that CD8 cells depleted by immunosuppression can regenerate quickly, whereas the process of making new CD4 cells is very slow.

T-Cell Receptors: Recognizing Both HLA and Antigen

T-cell TCR diversity is as important as HLA polymorphism. What’s more, the TCR is bound to recognize both the HLA on the APC that encountered and recognized the antigen and the antigen that HLA carries.

The diversity of HLAs on APCs enables recognition of foreign antigens. The HLA on APCs is of two types- HLA-I and HLA-II- which recognize TCRs on CD8 and CD4 cells, respectively. Because MHC-I is far more abundant than MHC-II, CD8 cells play a larger role in disease resistance.

Thus, if the TCR cannot properly recognize both the HLA and the antigen it carries, the TCR (and even the antibody-making B cells) cannot function properly. As soon as the TCR detects a foreign antigen, the internal defensive machinery in every kind of T cell starts working.

The Work of Calcineurin and Immune Suppression

Regardless of T cell type, another key protein in the pathway switches on its internal machinery: calcineurin. It holds the key to the T cell’s ability, or machinery, to confront foreign substances and defend the body. If calcineurin is blocked, the T cell’s capacity can be eroded.

The immunosuppressants used in kidney or other organ transplants target this very calcineurin. Tacrolimus and cyclosporine act directly against calcineurin to weaken it. Drugs that block other cytokines produced when calcineurin is activated- including IL-2 and IL-6- have also recently started being used in medicine.

As already said above, if any of us needs an organ transplant, the body does not recognize the replaced organ right away at first. Immunosuppressants, including tacrolimus, are used so the body does not attack the new organ, and the transplant does not fail.

The question may come up again: aren’t T cells supposed to fight viruses and bacteria? Why would T cells attack a new kidney that had to be transplanted because both of the body’s own kidneys stopped working? A new kidney or other organ isn’t a disease-causing foreign substance like bacteria, viruses, or allergens- so why does the immune system turn on it?

Why Immune Suppression When Transplanting a Kidney or Other Organ?

There are two reasons our body’s T cells don’t attack any of our own organs. First, because the MHC combination on our APCs matches that of our organs, they don’t recognize our own organs as foreign substances. Second, regulatory T cells provide a second layer of protection. They have specific TCR sequences that recognize our body and are recognized only by them; if other T cells try to attack too much, they detect it at once and in turn attack those T cells and weaken them.

That is why it is said that, for any organ transplant, it is best to receive the organ from close relatives, when possible. The secret lies in HLA polymorphism in our DNA. This is because close relatives share more of their HLA sequences, and self-antigens may already have formed. Because of this closer HLA match, the closer the donor and recipient are, the lower the chance of transplant failure.

If the donor and recipient are twins, their HLA types match. In the rest of us, an HLA mismatch exists somewhere. The antigen-presenting cells (APCs in our bodies recognize this mismatch as a foreign antigen and prepare our T cells to fight it. Because T cells mistake the newly transplanted organ for a foreign antigen or a disease, they attack it, which can lead to organ rejection and transplant failure.

The secret lies hidden in the polymorphism of HLA in our DNA.

It has been said that the closer the donor and recipient, the smaller this danger. But we must not forget that the danger exists for everyone. Even when the donor and recipient are twins with a complete HLA match, the risk that the transplanted organ will be rejected for various reasons remains, though it is somewhat smaller. It is to prevent this very transplant failure, which can happen to anyone who has had a transplant, that immunosuppressant drugs, including tacrolimus, have to be taken for life.

All medicines and their side effects cannot be lumped together and discussed in one breath. For a physician who has worked in this field for a long time to make an absurd pronouncement is even more shameful. My knowledge is limited; I don’t know much about the inner workings of drugs. I knew about the immune system, immunosuppressants, and PTLD, so I wrote. The doctor sahib I discussed above, but did not name, has done a great deal of work on this subject. He certainly ought to know about side effects and the sensitivity of the words he used. It would be better if experienced people in medicine didn’t start talking loosely the moment they see a crowd and a camera.

  • Cancer Is Beaten in Mice. When in Humans?

title.$t: Why Don’t Elephants Get Cancer the Way Humans Do?

content.$t:
Even though large animals like elephants have billions of cells, cancer is rare in them, while in humans its risk is notably higher. What could be the reason? Let us be clear from the start: the evolutionary reasons…

Large animals like elephants avert this danger by increasing the number of cancer-resistant genes. Because humans have limited genetic diversity, they could not develop such a strong defense mechanism.

This article was first published in Nepali on [Ukaalo](https://www.ukaalo.com/news/30229/) on November 2, 2025 (Kartik 16, 2082 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: [ukaalo.com ↗](https://www.ukaalo.com/news/30229/)

Even though large animals like elephants have billions of cells, cancer is rare in them, while in humans its risk is notably higher. What could be the reason? Let us be clear from the start: the evolutionary reasons behind the different cancer-resistance capacities of elephants and humans, along with differences in genetic diversity, have shaped their ability to resist disease.

Cancer and Body Size: Peto’s Paradox

For a long time, cancer was understood as a problem caused by mutations in cells. As DNA mutations gradually accumulate in each cell, a tumor capable of causing cancer may form. By that logic, the more cells an animal has, the more cancer it should get. But reality is the opposite: the cancer rate is roughly the same across small animals such as mice and large ones such as elephants and whales. In fact, in large animals like elephants and whales, the cancer rate is far lower than in humans.

In the 1970s, the British biologist Richard Peto studied the relationship between age and cancer in mice. Adding body size to the equation, he posed a question: the human body has nearly a thousand times more cells than a mouse’s and a lifespan 30 times longer, so why is there no comparably large difference in cancer likelihood between the two species? In theory, humans should carry a far greater cancer risk than mice—so why isn’t that the case?

One of the most intriguing and fundamental questions in the study of cancer is Peto’s Paradox. This paradox highlights an important idea: cancer is not simply a product of how many cells an organism has, but the result of genetic mechanisms preserved over the course of a species’ evolution.

The Elephant’s Evolutionary Defense Against Cancer: Copies of P53

The elephants found today in Africa and Asia have bodies up to nearly a hundred times larger than ours, with correspondingly more cells. But elephants were not always this big; they evolved from smaller ancestors. The oldest known elephant ancestor is said to have lived nearly 60 million years ago and weighed at most around 10 kilograms. The large size of the elephants we see today emerged about 10 million years ago.

Cancer is not simply a product of how many cells an organism has, but the result of genetic mechanisms preserved over a species’ evolution.

Almost all animals have a protein called P53 in every cell of their bodies. The human body carries only one copy of P53. The main role of the P53 protein in a cell is to detect DNA damage and stop that cell from dividing, or, if necessary, trigger the cell’s self-destruction (apoptosis). When biologists studied the DNA of elephants and their ancestors, they found something interesting: as the elephant’s body grew larger, the number of copies (copy number) of the gene that encodes P53 on its chromosomes also increased.

Alongside its enormous body and long lifespan, the elephant developed this mechanism for making extra copies of the gene as a genetic (evolutionary) adaptation to lower its cancer risk. The oldest elephant ancestor had only a single copy of P53, just like us. As elephants evolved and grew larger, the number of copies of the genes that make P53 also increased, and today’s elephants carry about 20 copies of P53 (13) when P53-like genes (P63, P73) are counted together. In this way, the extra copies of P53 in elephants help prevent cancer by triggering cell self-destruction as soon as a cell’s DNA is damaged.

Making extra copies of P53, however, is not the only strategy for surviving cancer. Over the course of their evolution, elephants, whales, and other species have developed cancer-resistant systems—gene duplication, enhanced tumor-suppressor activity, and strengthened pathways, including DNA-repair mechanisms. That is why, even in today’s polluted environment, cancer is only rarely the leading cause of death in large animals like elephants and whales, or in long-lived animals like tortoises.

So why couldn’t the human species develop the ability to fight cancer?

Limited Genetic Diversity in Humans: The Genetic Bottleneck

Although the human species is physically small, vast in number, and spread across every landmass, our genetic diversity is surprisingly limited. The genetic difference between any two unrelated people anywhere in the world averages only 0.1%. Compare this to the chimpanzee, the closest relative of our species (Homo sapiens). The genetic difference among chimpanzees in eastern and western Africa alone averages 1.2%. In other words, the difference between two chimpanzees from Africa alone is ten times greater than the difference between people from Europe, Asia, the Americas, and Africa. The secret behind this shrinking of diversity in human DNA lies in the evolutionary history of our species.

Humans and chimpanzees are believed to have diverged from a common ancestor nearly 5 million years ago. Based on the evidence found so far, Homo sapiens is estimated to have diverged from other contemporary human species (Neanderthals and Denisovans) roughly 500,000–800,000 years ago. The oldest evidence of Homo sapiens comes from several places (Morocco, South Africa) and dates back nearly 300,000 years. Sister species that left Africa as early as 400,000 years ago and reached Asia and Europe reunited with Homo sapiens only 40,000–50,000 years ago—and evidence of that reunion is still found in many of us living outside Africa.

The difference between two chimpanzees from Africa alone is ten times greater than the difference between people from Europe, Asia, the Americas and Africa.

Humans are thought to have lived in Africa for a long time, venturing out sporadically only about 100,000 years ago. Living in small groups across different parts of Africa, our ancestors gradually developed genetic diversity suited to their local environments. That is why most of the variation within our average 0.1% genetic diversity is still found in Africa today.

What Caused the Bottleneck in Human Evolution? The Toba Eruption

When we study the history of human evolution, we find clear evidence that the population of human ancestors—who evolved for a long time in diverse environments across Africa—dropped sharply at various points. Many scientific studies hold that roughly 70,000–80,000 years ago, the ‘effective population size’ of humans capable of reproducing fell so far that no more than 2,000–10,000 survived.

This severe genetic bottleneck in human history did not merely reduce the number of our ancestors; it permanently changed our genetic makeup.

When we examine the reasons for the extremely low genetic diversity in humans, we find genetic evidence of a bottleneck around 70,000 to 100,000 years ago. Many believe the eruption of the Toba volcano in Sumatra, Indonesia, about 74,000 years ago caused it.

This severe genetic bottleneck in human history did not merely reduce the number of our ancestors; it permanently changed our genetic makeup.

This eruption, the largest known so far, released huge amounts of sulfur gas into the atmosphere and brought a ‘volcanic winter’ to the world for many years. One school of thought holds that the sudden drop in temperature and the food crisis caused by the lack of sunlight reduced the effective population size of humans. However, because other human sister species living in Asia itself did not decline much, Toba cannot be accepted as the definitive cause of the bottleneck.

What Caused the Bottleneck in Human Evolution? The Founder Effect

An important cause of the genetic bottleneck is the founder effect that arose during migration out of Africa. There is also a genetic basis for the view that a very small group of humans left Africa and spread through Asia and Europe to the rest of the world. Similarities are found in mitochondrial DNA (small structures within the cell), which is passed from a woman’s egg/embryo to all of her offspring, and in the Y chromosome found in all men.

There is also a view that everyone outside Africa descends from a single shared mother and father. Biologists sometimes call this common mother and father ‘Mitochondrial Eve’ and ‘Chromosomal Adam,’ respectively. One way to understand this is that only a small founding group from Africa left Africa, and today’s modern humans are descended from them. The reduced genetic diversity seen in non-Africans today is largely the result of this founder effect.

There is a great deal of uniformity in our species, but our deep genetic history makes the story of our evolution even more complex. As this small ancestral group that left Africa about 60,000–70,000 years ago pushed into new regions, smaller subgroups split off at each location. Each migrating subgroup carried only a small fraction of the original population as it spread into new regions, first into Asia and Europe.

As humans spread across the world, the gradual extinction of early subgroups also helped reduce genetic diversity in modern humans. Because of this gradual process, even though our species has spread across the globe, our genetic diversity is far lower than that of other mammal species.

By facing similar bottlenecks during evolution and with a limited founding group leaving Africa, the human species escaped extinction—yet this same history affected our innate ability to fight diseases like cancer.

The Evidence for Bottlenecks in Human Evolution

Although that small founding group, some 45,000–60,000 years ago, saved humankind from extinction, it can be said that it is also the reason our innate ability to fight diseases like cancer was affected.

So when we study the DNA of our species after it left Africa, we find solid evidence of the genetic bottleneck: the very low number of genes, the tendency of genes to stay together, and the time at which genes converge. We did not learn that such a bottleneck once existed from studying ancestral skeletons; biologists discovered it by investigating DNA.

When human DNA is compared with that of many other mammals, the number of genes turns out to be very low—only about thirty thousand in total. This low gene count can be understood as the result of our species evolving gradually from a small number of ancestors, with most rare genes lost forever along with the ancestors who disappeared. Another sign that our species came from a limited set of ancestors is the tendency of genes to stay together (linkage disequilibrium). Genes on a chromosome normally separate gradually as they are passed down each generation. But when the ancestral population is small, this process is much slower. As a result, segments of genes on our chromosomes that should have long since separated are still found linked together today.

Another basis for the genetic bottleneck is the time at which genes converge (coalescence time). When we trace any gene in our DNA backward, all its copies converge on a single common ancestor. When a population is small, this ‘convergence time’ is very short. Analyses of modern human genes show that all our ancestors evolved from a single small group a relatively short time ago, supporting the idea of a breeding population numbering only a few thousand.

Narrowed Genetic Diversity and the Link to Cancer

The most significant consequence of the bottleneck in human evolution is genetic drift. As people split into small subgroups and settled in different places, the likelihood of inbreeding increased. In a large population, natural selection can easily remove harmful mutations (deleterious mutations)—a possibility our evolutionary history took away.

Inbreeding, or the practice of marrying within one’s own community, is still seen among modern humans. Some mutations that raise cancer risk (for example, certain defects in tumor-suppressor genes) remain in an inactive state. Inbreeding increases the chance that previously hidden or inactive (recessive) harmful genes appear together in offspring. Another aspect is that, because of these bottlenecks, the frequency of such harmful genes in the population has kept rising.

Large animals like elephants averted this danger by increasing the number of cancer-resistant genes (such as extra copies of the P53 gene). Likewise, the whale, another giant species, has built additional mechanisms to fight DNA mutation or damage. Because of the limited genetic diversity of the human species, such a strong defense mechanism could not develop.

Narrowed MHC Diversity and the Link to Cancer

The effect of the bottleneck in our species is not limited to new mutations arising through genetic drift. The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is a group of important genes tied to the immune system’s defense against cancer and other diseases; in humans, it is called the human leukocyte antigen (HLA). These genes play a key role in helping the body’s cells recognize and distinguish ‘self’ from ‘foreign’ (such as cancer cells and viruses).

These MHCs act as ‘molecular ID cards’ that help recognize viruses, bacteria, and tumor cells—the more variants a population carries, the greater its chance of developing an effective immune system. Cancerous cells produce abnormal or mutated proteins; HLA molecules capture fragments of these proteins and display them on the outer surface of the cells that fight cancer (T cells).

Because MHC diversity has been a central pillar of disease resistance throughout evolution, these genes are the most polymorphic—that is, the most diverse—in the entire genome. But this is exactly where the human problem shows up: in most of us, HLA diversity is very limited. Moreover, HLA diversity is much higher in Africa’s indigenous populations, whereas in groups that left Africa, its range has gradually declined.

As a result of the genetic bottleneck, reduced HLA diversity limits the ability to present each cancer-derived fragment. As HLA genetic diversity falls, the likelihood of having HLA molecules that can recognize new or unusual cancer mutations, confront cancer, and present them to T cells gradually declines. This gradual erosion of MHC can be understood as ‘holes’ in immune recognition. Because HLA diversity is low in our species, the risk of cancer developing and spreading can be unusually high compared with other mammals.

Peto’s Paradox, Narrowed Genetic Diversity, and Cancer

All in all, cancer is not merely a rebellion of the body’s cells; it is also the shadow of a paradox left by our species’ evolutionary history. Despite having billions of cells, large animals like elephants and whales evolved mechanisms that lower cancer risk—more copies of the P53 gene, additional DNA-repair systems, and doubled tumor-suppressor activity. Humans lost that evolutionary opportunity because of genetic bottlenecks for various reasons.

The paradox Peto observed between mice and humans is also interesting. In mice, cells divide rapidly, life is short, and the mutation rate is high—so tumors appear quickly. Because humans live a long time, tumors develop slowly, and the immune system has to confront them over a long period. When the diversity of MHC and DNA-repair mechanisms is limited, that very long lifespan becomes a new weakness: the body cannot control the cumulative consequences of mutation.

Cancer is not merely a rebellion of the body’s cells; it is also the shadow of a paradox left behind by our species’ evolutionary history.

So Peto’s Paradox is not just a paradox between species; it is also a paradox within us. We have intellectually advanced brains and the ability to develop medicines, but in evolutionary terms we are still descendants of a small, genetically limited group—and because of that, we lost the chance to develop the biological shields that guard against diseases like cancer.

Read also

  • Lobsters Don’t Age: Telomerase, Telomeres and the Price of Living Forever
  • Cancer Is Beaten in Mice. When in Humans?
  • The Architecture of a Cure
